chapters.title: Chapter 1 — How Candide Was Brought Up in a Magnificent Castle, and How He Was Expelled Thence
paragraphs: In a castle in Westphalia belonging to the Baron of Thunder-ten-Tronckh, there lived a young man whom nature had endowed with the gentlest manners. His face was a true picture of his soul. He combined sound judgment with simplicity of spirit, which is the reason, I believe, that he was called Candide. The old servants of the household suspected he was the son of the Baron's sister by a kind and honest gentleman of the neighborhood, a man the young lady had refused to marry because he could prove only seventy-one quarterings of nobility, the rest of his family tree having been lost to the ravages of time.

The Baron was one of the most powerful lords in Westphalia, for his castle had not only a gate but windows. His great hall was even hung with tapestry. All the dogs in his farmyards could be mustered into a pack of hounds when needed; his grooms served as his huntsmen; and the village curate was his grand almoner. They called him "My Lord" and laughed at all his jokes.

The Baron's wife weighed about three hundred and fifty pounds and was therefore a woman of great consequence, and she did the honors of the house with a dignity that commanded even greater respect. Her daughter Cunegonde was seventeen, rosy, pretty, plump, and desirable. The Baron's son appeared in every way worthy of his father. The tutor Pangloss was the oracle of the household, and little Candide listened to his lessons with all the innocent trust of his age and character.

Pangloss was a professor of metaphysico-theologico-cosmolo-nigology. He proved admirably that there is no effect without a cause, and that in this best of all possible worlds the Baron's castle was the most magnificent of castles, and his lady the best of all possible Baronesses.

"It is demonstrable," he said, "that things cannot be other than as they are; for since everything is made for a purpose, everything is necessarily made for the best purpose. Notice that noses were made to wear spectacles—and so we have spectacles. Legs are clearly designed for stockings—and we have stockings. Stones were made to be cut and used to build castles—therefore my lord has a magnificent castle, for the greatest baron in the province ought to be the best housed. Pigs were made to be eaten—therefore we eat pork all year round. Consequently, those who claim that all is well have said something foolish; they should have said that all is for the best."

Candide listened attentively and believed innocently, for he thought Miss Cunegonde extraordinarily beautiful, though he never had the courage to tell her so. He concluded that after the happiness of being born the Baron of Thunder-ten-Tronckh, the second greatest happiness was to be Miss Cunegonde, the third was to see her every day, and the fourth was to hear Master Pangloss, the greatest philosopher of the whole province, and consequently of the whole world.

One day Cunegonde, walking near the castle in a little wood they called a park, spotted Dr. Pangloss between the bushes giving a lesson in experimental natural philosophy to her mother's chambermaid, a pretty, docile little brunette. Since Miss Cunegonde had a great aptitude for the sciences, she watched breathlessly the repeated experiments she witnessed; she clearly grasped the force of the Doctor's arguments, the effects, and the causes. She walked back greatly flustered, quite pensive, and filled with the desire to be learned, imagining that she might well serve as a sufficient reason for young Candide, and he for her.

She met Candide on returning to the castle and blushed; Candide blushed too; she wished him good morning in a faltering voice, and Candide spoke to her without knowing what he said. The next day, after dinner, as they left the table, Cunegonde and Candide found themselves behind a screen; Cunegonde dropped her handkerchief, Candide picked it up, she innocently took his hand, the young man innocently kissed the young lady's hand with particular vivacity, feeling, and grace; their lips met, their eyes sparkled, their knees trembled, their hands wandered. Baron Thunder-ten-Tronckh happened to pass near the screen, and seeing this cause and effect, he drove Candide from the castle with great kicks to the backside; Cunegonde fainted; the Baroness boxed her ears as soon as she came to; and all was consternation in this most magnificent and most agreeable of all possible castles.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — What Became of Candide Among the Bulgarians
paragraphs: Candide, driven from this earthly paradise, walked a long time without knowing where he was going, weeping, raising his eyes to heaven, and turning them often toward the most magnificent of castles that now held prisoner the purest of noble young ladies. He lay down to sleep without supper in the middle of a field between two furrows. The snow fell in large flakes. The next day Candide, half frozen, dragged himself toward the neighboring town, which was called Waldberghofftrarbk-dikdorff. He had no money and was dying of hunger and exhaustion, so he stopped sorrowfully at the door of an inn. Two men dressed in blue noticed him.
"Comrade," said one, "here's a well-built young fellow, and the right height."
They approached Candide and very politely invited him to dinner.
"Gentlemen," replied Candide, with the most charming modesty, "you do me great honor, but I have no way to pay my share."
"Oh, sir," said one of the men in blue, "people of your appearance and your merit never pay for anything. Aren't you five feet five inches tall?"
"Yes, sir, that is my height," he answered with a low bow.
"Come now, sir, sit down. Not only will we pay your bill, but we'll never let a man like you want for money. Men were put on earth to help one another."
"You're right," said Candide. "That's exactly what Mr. Pangloss always taught me, and I see clearly that all is for the best."
They urged him to accept a few crowns. He took them and tried to give them an IOU; they refused; they sat down at the table.
"Don't you deeply love—"
"Oh yes," he answered, "I deeply love Miss Cunegonde."
"No," said one of the gentlemen, "we're asking whether you deeply love the King of the Bulgarians."
"Not at all," he said, "for I have never seen him."
"What! He is the best of kings, and we must drink his health."
"Oh, most willingly, gentlemen," and he drank.
"That's enough," they told him. "Now you are the supporter, the defender, the hero of the Bulgarians. Your fortune is made, and your glory is assured."

They immediately clapped him in irons and dragged him off to the regiment. There he was made to face right, face left, draw his ramrod, return his ramrod, present arms, fire, march—and they gave him thirty strokes with a cudgel. The next day he did his drill a little less badly and received only twenty strokes. The day after that they gave him only ten, and his comrades regarded him as a prodigy.

Candide, utterly dazed, could not yet quite understand how he had become a hero. One fine spring day he decided to go for a walk, marching straight ahead, believing that it was a privilege of the human species, as well as of the animal, to use its legs as it pleased. He had gone two leagues when he was overtaken by four other heroes, each six feet tall, who tied him up and hauled him off to a dungeon. He was asked which he preferred: to be whipped thirty-six times through the whole regiment, or to receive twelve lead balls in his brain all at once. He protested in vain that the human will is free and that he chose neither. He was forced to choose; and by virtue of that gift from God called liberty, he decided to run the gauntlet thirty-six times. He endured this twice. The regiment consisted of two thousand men; that made four thousand strokes for him, which laid bare all his muscles and nerves from the nape of his neck down to his buttocks. As they were about to proceed to a third whipping, Candide, unable to bear any more, begged them as a favor to be so kind as to shoot him. He was granted this favor; they bandaged his eyes and made him kneel. At that very moment the King of the Bulgarians passed by and inquired about the nature of the prisoner's crime. Since he had great talent, he understood from everything he learned about Candide that he was a young metaphysician utterly ignorant of the ways of this world, and he granted him a pardon with a clemency that will earn him praise in all the newspapers and throughout all the ages.

A skilled surgeon cured Candide in three weeks with emollients prescribed by Dioscorides. He had already grown a little new skin and was able to march when the King of the Bulgarians gave battle to the King of the Abarians.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — How Candide Made His Escape from the Bulgarians, and What Afterwards Became of Him
paragraphs: There was never anything so dashing, so smart, so brilliant, and so well-ordered as the two armies. Trumpets, fifes, oboes, drums, and cannons made music such as Hell itself had never heard. The cannons first laid flat about six thousand men on each side; the muskets swept from this best of worlds nine or ten thousand scoundrels who had been infesting its surface. The bayonet was also a sufficient reason for the death of several thousand more. The total might come to thirty thousand souls. Candide, who trembled like a philosopher, hid himself as well as he could during this heroic butchery.

At last, while the two kings each had a Te Deum sung in his own camp, Candide decided to go and reason elsewhere about causes and effects. He walked over heaps of the dead and dying and first reached a nearby village; it lay in ashes—it was an Abarian village that the Bulgarians had burned in accordance with the laws of war. Here, old men covered with wounds watched their wives, clutching their children to their bloody breasts, being massacred before their eyes; there, their daughters, disemboweled and drawing their last breath after satisfying the natural needs of Bulgarian heroes; while others, half-burned in the flames, begged to be finished off. The ground was strewn with brains, arms, and legs.

Candide fled quickly to another village; it belonged to the Bulgarians, and the Abarian heroes had treated it the same way. Candide, walking all the while over quivering limbs or across ruins, at last arrived beyond the theater of war, with a few provisions in his knapsack and Miss Cunegonde always in his heart. His provisions ran out when he arrived in Holland, but having heard that everyone in that country was rich, and that they were Christians, he had no doubt he would meet with the same treatment there as he had received in the Baron's castle before Miss Cunegonde's bright eyes became the cause of his expulsion.
He begged for alms from several serious-looking people, who all answered that if he kept up this trade they would lock him in the house of correction, where he would be taught how to earn a living.
The next person he approached was a man who had been haranguing a large assembly for a whole hour on the subject of charity. But the orator, looking at him sideways, said:
"What are you doing here? Are you on the side of the good cause?"

"There can be no effect without a cause," answered Candide modestly. "The whole is necessarily linked together and arranged for the best. It was necessary that I should be banished from the presence of Miss Cunegonde, that I should afterward run the gauntlet, and that I should now beg my bread until I learn how to earn it. None of this could have been otherwise."
"My friend," said the orator to him, "do you believe the Pope to be the Antichrist?"
"I have not heard as much," answered Candide; "but whether he is or is not, I need bread."
"You don't deserve to eat," said the other. "Be off, you rogue; be off, you wretch; never come near me again."

The orator's wife, poking her head out the window and spotting a man who doubted whether the Pope was the Antichrist, emptied over him a full…. Oh, heavens! To what excess does religious zeal carry the ladies.

A man who had never been christened, a good Anabaptist named James, witnessed the cruel and disgraceful treatment being given to one of his fellow creatures, a featherless biped with a rational soul. He took him home, cleaned him up, gave him bread and beer, presented him with two florins, and even offered to teach him the manufacture of the Persian fabrics that are made in Holland. Candide, almost throwing himself at his feet, cried:
"Master Pangloss said it well: all is for the best in this world, for I am infinitely more moved by your extreme generosity than by the inhumanity of that gentleman in the black coat and his lady."

The next day, as he was taking a walk, he met a beggar covered in scabs, with diseased eyes, the tip of his nose eaten away, his mouth twisted out of shape, his teeth black, choking in his throat, tormented by a violent cough, and spitting out a tooth with each effort.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — How Candide Found His Old Master Pangloss, and What Happened to Them
paragraphs: Candide, moved more by compassion than by horror, gave this shocking beggar the two florins he had received from the honest Anabaptist James. The specter stared at him intently, shed a few tears, and fell on his neck. Candide recoiled in disgust.
"Alas!" said one wretch to the other, "don't you recognize your dear Pangloss anymore?"

"What do I hear? You, my dear master! You in this terrible state! What misfortune has befallen you? Why are you no longer in the most magnificent of castles? What has become of Miss Cunegonde, the pearl of young women, nature's masterpiece?"
"I am so weak I cannot stand," said Pangloss.
Whereupon Candide carried him to the Anabaptist's stable and gave him a crust of bread. As soon as Pangloss had recovered a little:
"Well," said Candide, "what about Cunegonde?"
"She is dead," replied the other.
Candide fainted at this word; his friend revived him with a little bad vinegar he happened to find in the stable. Candide reopened his eyes.
"Cunegonde dead! Ah, best of worlds, where are you? But what illness did she die of? Wasn't it from grief at seeing her father kick me out of his magnificent castle?"

"No," said Pangloss, "she was ripped open by the Bulgarian soldiers after being raped by many; they broke the Baron's head for trying to defend her; my lady her mother was cut to pieces; my poor pupil was treated in just the same way as his sister; and as for the castle, they didn't leave one stone on top of another—not a barn, not a sheep, not a duck, not a tree. But we have had our revenge, for the Abarians have done exactly the same to a neighboring barony that belonged to a Bulgarian lord."

At this account Candide fainted again; but on coming to himself and saying everything he ought to say, he inquired into the cause and effect, and into the sufficient reason that had reduced Pangloss to so miserable a state.
"Alas!" said the other, "it was love—love, comfort of the human species, preserver of the universe, soul of all feeling beings, tender love."

"Alas!" said Candide, "I know this love, that sovereign of hearts, that soul of our souls; and yet it never cost me more than a kiss and twenty kicks on the backside. How could this beautiful cause produce in you so abominable an effect?"

Pangloss answered in these terms: "Oh, my dear Candide, you remember Paquette, that pretty servant girl who attended our noble Baroness; in her arms I tasted the delights of paradise, which produced in me these torments of hell you see devouring me. She was infected with them; perhaps she has died of them. She received this present from a learned Franciscan friar, who had traced it back to its source; he had it from an old countess, who had received it from a cavalry captain, who owed it to a marchioness, who took it from a page, who had received it from a Jesuit, who as a novice had it in a direct line from one of Christopher Columbus's companions. For my part, I shall give it to no one—I am dying."
"Oh, Pangloss!" cried Candide, "what a strange genealogy! Isn't the Devil the original source of it?"

"Not at all," replied this great man. "It was an unavoidable thing, a necessary ingredient in the best of worlds; for if Columbus had not caught on an island in America this disease, which contaminates the source of life, frequently even prevents reproduction, and which is plainly contrary to the great purpose of nature, we would have neither chocolate nor cochineal. We must also observe that on our continent this affliction, like religious controversy, is confined to a particular region. The Turks, the Indians, the Persians, the Chinese, the Siamese, the Japanese know nothing of it; but there is sufficient reason to believe that they will know it in their turn within a few centuries. Meanwhile, it has made marvelous progress among us, especially in those great armies made up of honest, well-disciplined mercenaries who decide the fate of nations; for we can safely say that when an army of thirty thousand men fights another of equal size, there are about twenty thousand cases of pox on each side."
"Well, this is wonderful!" said Candide; "but you must get cured."
"Alas! How can I?" said Pangloss. "I haven't a penny, my friend, and nowhere on earth can you have blood let or a clyster administered without paying, or someone paying for you."

These last words decided Candide; he went and threw himself at the feet of the charitable Anabaptist James, and gave him so touching an account of the state his friend had been reduced to that the good man did not hesitate to take Dr. Pangloss into his house and have him cured at his own expense. In the cure Pangloss lost only an eye and an ear. He wrote well and knew arithmetic perfectly. The Anabaptist James made him his bookkeeper. After two months, having to go to Lisbon on some mercantile business, he took the two philosophers along with him on his ship. Pangloss explained to him how everything was so constituted that it could not be better. James was not of this opinion.

"It is more likely," he said, "that mankind has somewhat corrupted its nature, for men were not born wolves, and they have become wolves. God gave them neither twenty-four-pound cannons nor bayonets, and yet they have made cannons and bayonets to destroy one another. On this account I might mention not only bankrupts, but also the Justice that seizes the assets of bankrupts to defraud their creditors."
"All this was indispensable," replied the one-eyed doctor, "for private misfortunes make up the general good, so that the more private misfortunes there are, the greater is the general good."
While he was reasoning, the sky darkened, the winds blew from all four quarters, and the ship was battered by a most terrible tempest within sight of the port of Lisbon.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — Tempest, Shipwreck, Earthquake, and What Became of Doctor Pangloss, Candide, and James the Anabaptist
paragraphs: Half-dead from the inconceivable agony produced by a ship's pitching, half the passengers were not even aware of the danger. The other half shrieked and prayed. The sails were ripped, the masts broken, the hull split open. Whoever wanted to work at it, no one listened, no one gave orders. The Anabaptist was on deck lending a hand when a brutish sailor struck him roughly and knocked him sprawling; but with the force of the blow the sailor himself tumbled headfirst overboard and caught on a piece of the broken mast. Honest James ran to his aid, hauled him up, and from the effort he made was thrown into the sea in full sight of the sailor, who left him to drown without deigning to glance at him. Candide came near and saw his benefactor rise above the water for a moment before being swallowed up forever. He was just about to leap after him when he was prevented by the philosopher Pangloss, who demonstrated to him that the Bay of Lisbon had been made on purpose so that the Anabaptist could be drowned in it. While he was proving this a priori, the ship foundered; all perished except Pangloss, Candide, and that brutal sailor who had drowned the good Anabaptist. The villain swam safely to shore, while Pangloss and Candide were carried there on a plank.

As soon as they had recovered a little, they walked toward Lisbon. They had some money left, with which they hoped to save themselves from starvation, having escaped drowning. Barely had they reached the city, lamenting the death of their benefactor, when they felt the ground tremble under their feet. The sea heaved and foamed in the harbor, smashing the vessels at anchor to pieces. Whirlwinds of fire and ashes swept through the streets and public squares; houses collapsed, roofs were flung down onto the pavement, and the pavement itself was torn apart. Thirty thousand inhabitants of all ages and both sexes were crushed beneath the ruins. The sailor, whistling and swearing, said there was plunder to be had here.
"What can be the sufficient reason for this phenomenon?" said Pangloss.
"This is the Last Day!" cried Candide.

The sailor ran in among the ruins, facing death to find money; finding it, he took it, got drunk, and having slept himself sober, purchased the favors of the first good-natured woman he met on the ruins of the demolished houses, in the midst of the dying and the dead. Pangloss tugged him by the sleeve.
"My friend," he said, "this is not right. You are sinning against universal reason; you are picking a bad moment."
"Blood and guts!" the other answered. "I am a sailor, born in Batavia. I have trampled on the crucifix four times in four voyages to Japan; to hell with your universal reason!"
Some falling stones had wounded Candide. He lay stretched out in the street, covered in rubble.
"Alas!" he said to Pangloss, "get me a little wine and oil; I am dying."

"This shaking of the earth is nothing new," answered Pangloss. "The city of Lima, in America, experienced the same convulsions last year; same cause, same effects. There must certainly be a vein of sulfur underground running from Lima to Lisbon."
"Nothing more probable," said Candide; "but for the love of God, a little oil and wine."
"What do you mean, probable?" the philosopher replied. "I maintain the point is capable of being demonstrated."

Candide fainted, and Pangloss fetched him some water from a nearby fountain. The next day they foraged among the ruins and found provisions, with which they restored their exhausted strength. Afterward they joined others in helping the inhabitants who had escaped death. Some of those they had helped gave them as good a dinner as could be managed in such disastrous circumstances; the meal, it is true, was mournful, and the guests moistened their bread with tears; but Pangloss consoled them, assuring them that things could not be otherwise.
"For," he said, "all that is is for the best. If there is a volcano at Lisbon, it cannot be anywhere else. It is impossible that things should be other than as they are; for everything is right."
A little man dressed in black, a Familiar of the Inquisition, who sat beside him, politely took up his words and said:
"Apparently, then, sir, you don't believe in original sin; for if all is for the best, then there has been neither Fall nor punishment."
"I humbly beg Your Excellency's pardon," answered Pangloss still more politely, "for the Fall of man and his curse necessarily entered into the system of the best of all possible worlds."
"Sir," said the Familiar, "then you do not believe in free will?"
"Your Excellency will forgive me," said Pangloss; "free will is consistent with absolute necessity, for it was necessary that we should be free; for, in short, the determined will—"
Pangloss was in the middle of his sentence when the Familiar gave a nod to his footman, who poured him a glass of wine from Porto, or Oporto.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — How the Portuguese Made a Beautiful Auto-da-fe, to Prevent Any Further Earthquakes; and How Candide Was Publicly Whipped
paragraphs: After the earthquake had destroyed three-quarters of Lisbon, the sages of that country could think of no more effective way to prevent utter ruin than to give the people a beautiful auto-da-fe; for it had been decided by the University of Coimbra that the burning of a few people alive over a slow fire, with great ceremony, is an infallible secret for keeping the earth from quaking.

Accordingly, they had arrested a Biscayan convicted of marrying his godmother, and two Portuguese for picking out the bacon that had been used to lard a chicken they were eating. After dinner they came and seized Dr. Pangloss and his disciple Candide—the one for having spoken his mind, the other for having listened with an air of approval. They were led to separate cells, extremely cold, where they were never troubled by the sun. Eight days later they were dressed in sanbenitos and their heads adorned with paper miters. The miter and sanbenito belonging to Candide were painted with inverted flames and with devils that had neither tails nor claws; but Pangloss's devils had claws and tails, and the flames were upright. Dressed like this, they marched in procession and listened to a very moving sermon followed by fine church music. Candide was whipped in time to the singing; the Biscayan and the two men who had refused to eat bacon were burned; and Pangloss was hanged, though that was not the usual custom. The same day the earth suffered another violent tremor.
Candide, terrified, stunned, despairing, bleeding, quivering all over, said to himself:

"If this is the best of all possible worlds, what are the others? Well, if I had only been whipped I could put up with it, for I went through that among the Bulgarians; but oh, my dear Pangloss, greatest of philosophers, that I should have seen you hanged without knowing why! Oh, my dear Anabaptist, best of men, that you should have been drowned in the very harbor! Oh, Miss Cunegonde, pearl of young women, that you should have had your belly ripped open!"
He was musing like this, scarcely able to stand, preached at, whipped, absolved, and blessed, when an old woman came up to him and said:
"My son, take courage and follow me."

chapters.title: Chapter 7 — How the Old Woman Took Care of Candide, and How He Found the Object He Loved
paragraphs: Candide did not take courage, but he followed the old woman to a run-down house, where she gave him a jar of ointment to rub on his wounds, showed him a very neat little bed with a suit of clothes hanging on the wall, and left him something to eat and drink.
"Eat, drink, sleep," she said, "and may Our Lady of Atocha, the great Saint Anthony of Padua, and the great Saint James of Compostela take you under their protection. I will be back tomorrow."
Candide, astonished at all he had suffered and still more at the old woman's kindness, tried to kiss her hand.
"It is not my hand you must kiss," said the old woman. "I will be back tomorrow. Rub yourself with the ointment, eat and sleep."

Candide, despite so many disasters, ate and slept. The next morning the old woman brought him his breakfast, examined his back, and rubbed it herself with another ointment; she brought him his dinner in the same way; and in the evening she returned with his supper. The next day she went through exactly the same routine.
"Who are you?" said Candide. "Who inspired you with so much kindness? How can I repay you?"
The good woman did not answer; she came back in the evening but brought no supper.
"Come with me," she said, "and say nothing."

She took him by the arm and walked with him about a quarter of a mile out into the country; they came to an isolated house surrounded by gardens and canals. The old woman knocked at a small door, it opened, and she led Candide up a private staircase into a small, richly furnished apartment. She left him on a brocaded sofa, shut the door, and went away. Candide thought he was dreaming; indeed, he thought he had been dreaming unluckily all his life, and that this present moment was the only agreeable part of it all.
The old woman returned very soon, helping along with difficulty a trembling woman of majestic figure, glittering with jewels and covered with a veil.
"Take off that veil," the old woman told Candide.

The young man approaches; with a timid hand he lifts the veil. Oh! what a moment! what astonishment! He thinks he sees Miss Cunegonde—he really sees her! It is she herself! His strength fails him, he cannot utter a word, and drops at her feet. Cunegonde falls on the sofa. The old woman produces a bottle of smelling salts; they come to themselves and recover their speech. They began with broken words, with questions and answers interrupted by turns with sighs, tears, and cries. The old woman asked them to make less noise, and then left them to themselves.
"What, is it you?" said Candide. "You are alive? I find you again in Portugal? Then you were not raped? Then they didn't rip open your belly, as Dr. Pangloss told me?"
"Yes, they did," said the beautiful Cunegonde; "but those two accidents are not always fatal."
"But were your father and mother killed?"
"It is all too true," answered Cunegonde in tears.
"And your brother?"
"My brother was killed too."
"And why are you in Portugal? And how did you know I was here? And by what strange adventure did you manage to have me brought to this house?"
"I will tell you all of that," replied the lady, "but first let me know your own story, from the innocent kiss you gave me and the kicks you received for it."

Candide obeyed her respectfully, and though he was still stunned, though his voice was feeble and trembling, though his back still hurt him, he gave her the most ingenuous account of everything that had happened to him since the moment of their separation. Cunegonde raised her eyes to heaven; she shed tears on hearing of the death of the good Anabaptist and of Pangloss; after which she spoke to Candide in the following terms, and he did not miss a word and devoured her with his eyes.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 — The History of Cunegonde
paragraphs: "I was in bed and fast asleep when it pleased God to send the Bulgarians to our delightful castle of Thunder-ten-Tronckh; they slaughtered my father and brother and cut my mother to pieces. A tall Bulgarian, six feet high, seeing that I had fainted at the sight, began to rape me; this brought me around. I regained my senses, I screamed, I struggled, I bit, I scratched, I tried to tear the tall Bulgarian's eyes out—not knowing that what was happening in my father's house was the usual custom of war. The brute gave me a gash in the left side with his sword, and the scar is still there."
"Ah! I hope I shall see it," said honest Candide.
"You shall," said Cunegonde, "but let us go on."
"Please do," replied Candide.
So she resumed the thread of her story:

"A Bulgarian captain came in, saw me all bleeding, and the soldier not in the least disturbed. The captain was enraged at the brute's disrespectful behavior and killed him on top of me. He ordered my wounds to be dressed and took me to his quarters as a prisoner of war. I washed what few shirts he had, I did his cooking; he thought me very pretty—he admitted as much; on the other hand, I must grant that he had a good figure and a soft, fair skin; but he had little or no mind or philosophy, and you could easily tell he had never been taught by Dr. Pangloss. After three months, having lost all his money and grown tired of my company, he sold me to a Jew named Don Issachar, who traded with Holland and Portugal and had a strong passion for women. This Jew was greatly attached to my person but could not triumph over it; I resisted him better than I had the Bulgarian soldier. A modest woman may be raped once, but her virtue is only strengthened by it. To make me more tractable, he brought me to this country house. Until then I had imagined nothing could equal the beauty of Thunder-ten-Tronckh Castle; but I found I was mistaken.

"The Grand Inquisitor, seeing me one day at Mass, stared at me for a long while and sent word that he wished to speak with me on private matters. I was conducted to his palace, where I told him the history of my family, and he pointed out to me how far beneath my rank it was to belong to an Israelite. A proposal was then put to Don Issachar that he should hand me over to his lordship. Don Issachar, being court banker and a man of credit, would hear nothing of it. The Inquisitor threatened him with an auto-da-fe. At last my Jew, intimidated, struck a bargain by which the house and I would belong to both in common: the Jew was to have for himself Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday, and the Inquisitor would have the rest of the week. It has now been six months since this arrangement was made. Quarrels have not been lacking, for they could not agree whether the night from Saturday to Sunday belonged to the old law or to the new. For my part, I have so far held out against both, and I truly believe this is the reason I am still loved.

"At last, to ward off the scourge of earthquakes and to intimidate Don Issachar, my Lord Inquisitor was pleased to hold an auto-da-fe. He did me the honor of inviting me to the ceremony. I had a very good seat, and the ladies were served refreshments between the Mass and the execution. I was indeed seized with horror at the burning of those two Jews and of the honest Biscayan who had married his godmother; but what was my surprise, my terror, my dismay, when I saw in a sanbenito and miter a figure that looked like Pangloss! I rubbed my eyes, I looked at him closely, I saw him hanged; I fainted. Scarcely had I recovered my senses than I saw you stripped stark naked, and this was the height of my horror, consternation, grief, and despair. I tell you frankly that your skin is still whiter and of a more perfect color than my Bulgarian captain's. This spectacle redoubled all the feelings that were overwhelming and devouring me. I cried out, and would have said, 'Stop, barbarians!' but my voice failed me, and my cries would have been useless after you had been severely whipped. How is it possible, I said to myself, that the beloved Candide and the wise Pangloss should both be at Lisbon, the one to receive a hundred lashes, the other to be hanged by order of the Grand Inquisitor, whose favorite I am? Pangloss deceived me most cruelly when he said that everything in the world is for the best.

"Agitated, distraught, sometimes beside myself, sometimes ready to die of weakness, my mind was filled with the massacre of my father, mother, and brother, with the insolence of the ugly Bulgarian soldier, with the stab he gave me, with my servitude under the Bulgarian captain, with my hideous Don Issachar, with my abominable Inquisitor, with the execution of Dr. Pangloss, with the grand Miserere chanted while you were whipped, and above all with the kiss I gave you behind the screen the day I last saw you. I thanked God for bringing you back to me after so many trials, and I instructed my old woman to take care of you and to bring you here as soon as possible. She has carried out her errand very well; I have tasted the inexpressible pleasure of seeing you again, of hearing you, of speaking with you. But you must be hungry; as for me, I am famished. Let us have supper."

They both sat down at table, and, when supper was over, they sat themselves again on the sofa, where they were when Signor Don Issachar arrived. It was the Jewish Sabbath, and Issachar had come to enjoy his rights and to declare his tender love.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 — What Became of Cunegonde, Candide, the Grand Inquisitor, and the Jew
paragraphs: This Issachar was the most hot-tempered Hebrew to be seen in Israel since the Captivity in Babylon.
"What!" he said, "you Galilean bitch, wasn't the Inquisitor enough for you? Does this scoundrel have to share with me too?"

Saying this, he drew a long dagger he always carried on him; and, not imagining that his opponent was armed, he flung himself at Candide. But our honest Westphalian had received a handsome sword from the old woman along with the suit of clothes. He drew his rapier, gentle as he was, and laid the Israelite stone dead on the cushions at Cunegonde's feet.
"Holy Virgin!" she cried, "what will become of us? A man killed in my apartment! If the officers of the law come, we're done for!"
"Had Pangloss not been hanged," said Candide, "he would give us good advice in this emergency, for he was a profound philosopher. In his absence, let us consult the old woman."

She was very prudent and was beginning to give her opinion when suddenly another little door opened. It was an hour past midnight, the beginning of Sunday. This day belonged to my lord the Inquisitor. He came in and saw the whipped Candide with sword in hand, a dead man on the floor, Cunegonde aghast, and the old woman offering counsel.
At that instant, here is what passed through Candide's soul, and how he reasoned:

If this holy man calls for help, he will certainly have me burned; and Cunegonde will perhaps meet the same fate; he was the cause of my being cruelly whipped; he is my rival; and, since I have now begun to kill, I shall kill on, for there is no time to hesitate. This reasoning was clear and instantaneous; so, without giving the Inquisitor time to recover from his surprise, he ran him through and through and laid him beside the Jew.
"Again!" said Cunegonde. "Now there is no mercy for us; we are excommunicated; our last hour has come. How could you do it—you, who are so naturally gentle—kill a Jew and a prelate in two minutes?"
"My beautiful young lady," answered Candide, "when a man is in love, jealous, and flogged by the Inquisition, he stops at nothing."
The old woman then spoke up and said:

"There are three Andalusian horses in the stable with bridles and saddles; let brave Candide get them ready; madam has money and jewels; let us mount quickly, though I can only sit on one buttock; let us set out for Cadiz. The weather is the finest in the world, and there is great pleasure in traveling in the cool of the night."

Candide immediately saddled the three horses, and he, Cunegonde, and the old woman covered thirty miles without stopping. While they were on their way, the Holy Brotherhood entered the house; my lord the Inquisitor was buried in a handsome church, and Issachar's body was thrown on a dunghill.
Candide, Cunegonde, and the old woman had now reached the little town of Avacena in the middle of the Sierra Morena mountains, and were speaking as follows in a public inn.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 — In What Distress Candide, Cunegonde, and the Old Woman Arrived at Cadiz; and of Their Embarkation
paragraphs: "Who can have robbed me of my money and jewels?" said Cunegonde, all bathed in tears. "How shall we live? What shall we do? Where shall we find Inquisitors or Jews who will give me more?"

"Alas!" said the old woman, "I have a strong suspicion of a reverend Franciscan friar who stayed in the same inn as us last night at Badajoz. God forbid I should judge rashly, but he came into our room twice, and he set out on his journey long before we did."

"Alas!" said Candide, "dear Pangloss has often proved to me that the goods of this world are common to all men, and that each has an equal right to them. But according to these principles, the Franciscan should have left us enough to finish our journey. Have you nothing at all left, my dear Cunegonde?"
"Not a penny," she said.
"What are we to do, then?" said Candide.
"Sell one of the horses," replied the old woman. "I will ride behind Miss Cunegonde, though I can only hold on with one buttock, and we shall reach Cadiz."

In the same inn there was a Benedictine prior who bought the horse cheaply. Candide, Cunegonde, and the old woman, having passed through Lucena, Chillas, and Lebrixa, arrived at last at Cadiz. A fleet was being fitted out there, and troops were assembling to bring to heel the reverend Jesuit Fathers of Paraguay, who were accused of inciting one of the native tribes near San Sacramento to revolt against the Kings of Spain and Portugal. Since Candide had served among the Bulgarians, he performed the military drills before the general of this little army with such grace of bearing, such a fearless air, and such agility and speed, that he was given command of a company of infantry. Now he was a captain! He set sail with Miss Cunegonde, the old woman, two servants, and the two Andalusian horses that had belonged to the Grand Inquisitor of Portugal.
During the voyage they debated a great deal about poor Pangloss's philosophy.

"We are going to another world," said Candide; "surely it must be there that all is for the best. For I must admit there is some reason to complain about what goes on in our own world, in both natural and moral philosophy."
"I love you with all my heart," said Cunegonde; "but my soul is still full of terror at what I have seen and endured."

"All will be well," replied Candide. "The sea of this new world is already better than our European sea; it is calmer, the winds more regular. It is surely the New World that is the best of all possible worlds."
"God grant it," said Cunegonde; "but I have been so horribly unhappy there that my heart is nearly closed to hope."
"You complain," said the old woman; "alas! you have not known misfortunes such as mine."
Cunegonde almost burst out laughing, finding the good woman very amusing for pretending to have been as unfortunate as herself.

"Alas!" said Cunegonde, "my good mother, unless you have been raped by two Bulgarians, received two deep wounds in your belly, had two castles demolished, had two mothers cut to pieces before your eyes, and two of your lovers whipped at an auto-da-fe, I don't see how you could be more unfortunate than I am. Add to that I was born a baroness of seventy-two quarterings—and I have worked as a cook!"
"Miss," replied the old woman, "you do not know my birth; and if I were to show you my backside, you would not speak like that, but would suspend your judgment."
This remark having aroused extreme curiosity in Cunegonde and Candide, the old woman spoke to them as follows.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 — History of the Old Woman
paragraphs: "I didn't always have bleary eyes and red eyelids. My nose didn't always touch my chin, and I wasn't always a servant. I'm the daughter of Pope Urban X and the Princess of Palestrina. Until I was fourteen I was raised in a palace that would have made every German baron's castle look like a stable. One of my gowns was worth more than all the splendor of Westphalia put together. As I grew up I became more beautiful, more witty, more graceful in every way, surrounded by pleasures, hopes, and respectful admiration. I was already inspiring love. My throat was fully formed — and what a throat! White, firm, shaped like the Venus de' Medici's. And such eyes! Such eyelids! Such black brows! My dark pupils shot flames that outshone the stars — so the local poets informed me. My maids went into ecstasy dressing and undressing me, whether they looked at me from the front or from behind. The gentlemen would have paid handsomely to trade places with them."

"I was engaged to the most distinguished Prince of Massa Carrara. What a prince! As handsome as I was, sweet-tempered, charming, brilliantly witty, and burning with love. I loved him the way one loves the first time — worshipfully, rapturously. The wedding was being arranged. The pomp and splendor were staggering. There were festivals, tournaments, endless comic operas. All of Italy composed sonnets in my honor, though not a single one was passable. I was just about to reach the summit of happiness when an old marchioness who had been my prince's mistress invited him over for hot chocolate. He died in less than two hours, in the most horrible convulsions. But this is a trifle. My mother, in despair and scarcely less broken than I was, decided to get away for a while from such a cursed place. She had a beautiful estate near Gaeta. We boarded a local galley, gilded like the great altar of St. Peter's in Rome. A Salé pirate ship swooped down and boarded us. Our men defended themselves like the Pope's soldiers do: they fell on their knees and threw down their weapons, begging the pirate for absolution in articulo mortis."

"In an instant they were stripped as bare as monkeys — and my mother, our maids of honor, and I were stripped the same way. It's astonishing how quickly those gentlemen can undress people. But what surprised me most was that they shoved their fingers into the part of our bodies which the general run of women reserve for a different instrument altogether. It struck me as a very strange ceremony — but that's how one judges things when one hasn't seen the world. I later learned it was to check whether we'd hidden any diamonds in there. It's the practice established from time immemorial among civilized nations that sail the seas. I was told that the very religious Knights of Malta never fail to perform this search when they capture Turkish prisoners of either sex. It's a law of nations from which they never deviate."

"I don't need to explain how hard it was for a young princess and her mother to be made slaves and hauled off to Morocco. You can easily imagine everything we suffered aboard the pirate ship. My mother was still very beautiful. Our maids of honor, and even our waiting women, had more charm than you'll find in all of Africa. As for me, I was ravishing — I was exquisite — grace itself — and I was a virgin. I did not remain one for long. That flower, which had been reserved for the handsome Prince of Massa Carrara, was plucked by the pirate captain. He was a repulsive Black man, and yet he thought he was doing me a tremendous honor. Certainly the Princess of Palestrina and I must have been very strong to endure everything we went through before reaching Morocco. But let's move on. These are such ordinary things they're hardly worth mentioning."

"Morocco was drowning in blood when we arrived. The fifty sons of the Emperor Muley-Ismael each had their own followers, which produced fifty civil wars — Black against Black, Black against brown, brown against brown, mulatto against mulatto. It was continuous slaughter throughout the empire."

"The moment we landed, Black soldiers from a faction opposing my captain's tried to rob him of his plunder. After the jewels and gold, we were his most valuable property. I witnessed a battle the likes of which you never see in your European climates. Northern peoples don't have that heat in their blood, that raging lust for women that is so common in Africa. You Europeans seem to have only milk in your veins, but it's vitriol, it's fire that runs in the veins of the people of the Atlas Mountains and the surrounding regions. They fought with the fury of the region's lions and tigers and serpents, to decide who would get us. A Moor grabbed my mother by the right arm, while my captain's lieutenant held her by the left. A Moorish soldier had one of her legs, one of our pirates the other. Almost every one of our women was pulled into quarters by four men at once. My captain kept me hidden behind him, and with his drawn scimitar slashed down anyone who dared oppose him. In the end I saw all of our Italian women, my mother included, torn, mangled, massacred by the monsters fighting over them. The slaves who were my companions, the men who'd captured them, the soldiers, sailors, Black men, white men, mulattoes — and at last my captain — all killed. And I was left dying on a heap of corpses. Scenes like this played out across three hundred leagues — and yet no one ever missed the five daily prayers ordained by Muhammad."

"With great effort I pulled myself out from under that heap of slaughtered bodies and crawled to a large orange tree on the bank of a little stream nearby, where I collapsed, overwhelmed by terror, exhaustion, horror, despair, and hunger. A moment later my shattered senses gave themselves up to sleep — a fainting more than a rest. I was in this state of weakness and unconsciousness, between life and death, when I felt something pressing down on me, something moving on my body. I opened my eyes and saw a white man, of pleasant appearance, who was sighing, and who was muttering between his teeth: 'O che sciagura d'essere senza coglioni!'"

chapters.title: Chapter 12 — The Adventures of the Old Woman Continued
paragraphs: "Astonished and delighted to hear my own language, and no less surprised by what this man was saying, I answered that there were far greater misfortunes than the one he complained of. I gave him a quick account of the horrors I'd endured and fainted a second time. He carried me to a nearby house, put me to bed, fed me, waited on me, consoled me, flattered me. He told me he'd never seen anyone as beautiful as me, and that he had never so much regretted the loss of what no one could ever recover."

"'I was born in Naples,' he said. 'There they castrate two or three thousand boys every year. Some die from the operation, others end up with voices more beautiful than a woman's, and others are raised to high offices of state. The operation was performed on me with great success, and I became chapel musician to madam, the Princess of Palestrina.'"
"'To my mother!' I cried."
"'Your mother!' he cried, weeping. 'What! Could you really be that little princess I raised until she was six, and who even then promised to be as beautiful as you are?'"
"'It's me, truly. But my mother lies four hundred yards from here, torn in quarters, under a heap of dead bodies.'"

"I told him the whole story of my adventures, and he told me his. He had been sent to the Emperor of Morocco by a Christian power to negotiate a treaty with that prince, under which he was to be furnished with weapons and ships to help destroy the trade of other Christian governments."
"'My mission is accomplished,' said this honest eunuch. 'I'm going to set sail for Ceuta, and I'll take you to Italy. Ma che sciagura d'essere senza coglioni!'"

"I thanked him with tears of gratitude. And instead of taking me to Italy, he took me to Algiers, where he sold me to the Dey. I'd scarcely been sold when the plague — which had been making the rounds of Africa, Asia, and Europe — broke out savagely in Algiers. You've seen earthquakes; but tell me, miss, have you ever had the plague?"
"Never," Cunegonde answered.

"If you had," said the old woman, "you'd admit it's far more terrible than any earthquake. It's common in Africa, and I caught it. Picture the miserable situation of a Pope's daughter, fifteen years old, who in less than three months had known the miseries of poverty and slavery, had been raped almost every day, had seen her mother pulled into quarters, had endured famine and war, and was now dying of plague in Algiers. I didn't die, though — but my eunuch did, and the Dey, and almost the entire harem of Algiers."

"As soon as the first fury of that terrible plague had spent itself, a sale of the Dey's slaves was held. A merchant bought me and took me to Tunis. He sold me to another merchant, who resold me to yet another in Tripoli. From Tripoli I was sold to Alexandria, from Alexandria to Smyrna, and from Smyrna to Constantinople. Eventually I became the property of an Aga of the Janissaries, who was soon ordered off to the defense of Azov, then under siege by the Russians."

"The Aga, who was a very gallant man, took his entire harem with him and lodged us in a little fort on the Sea of Azov, guarded by two Black eunuchs and twenty soldiers. The Turks killed prodigious numbers of Russians, but the Russians got their revenge. Azov was burned to the ground, its inhabitants put to the sword — no sex or age was spared — until only our little fort remained, and the enemy tried to starve us out. The twenty Janissaries had sworn they would never surrender. The extremes of famine they were reduced to forced them to eat our two eunuchs rather than break their oath. And within a few days they decided to devour the women as well."
"We had a very pious and humane Imam, who preached an excellent sermon urging them not to kill us all at once."

"'Just cut off a buttock from each of these ladies,' he said, 'and you'll dine extremely well. If you need more later, the same meal will be available in a few days. Heaven will accept such a charitable act and send you relief.'"
"He had great eloquence. He persuaded them. We underwent that terrible operation. The Imam applied to us the same balm he uses on children after circumcision. We all very nearly died."

"Scarcely had the Janissaries finished the meal we'd provided than the Russians arrived in flat-bottomed boats. Not one Janissary escaped. The Russians paid no attention to the state we were in. There are French surgeons everywhere in the world; a very clever one took us into his care and cured us. As long as I live I'll remember that as soon as my wounds had healed, he made advances at me. He told us all to cheer up, assuring us that the same thing had happened in many other sieges, and that it was according to the laws of war."

"As soon as my companions could walk, they were forced to set out for Moscow. I fell to the share of a Boyar who made me his gardener and gave me twenty lashes a day. But when this nobleman, along with thirty other Boyars, was broken on the wheel within two years for some court intrigue, I took advantage of the moment and fled. I crossed all of Russia. I was an innkeeper's servant for a long time at Riga, then at Rostock, Wismar, Leipzig, Kassel, Utrecht, Leiden, The Hague, Rotterdam. I grew old in misery and disgrace, with only half my backside, and always remembering I was a Pope's daughter. A hundred times I was on the point of killing myself — but I still loved life. This absurd weakness may be one of the most fatal traits we have. Is there anything more ridiculous than always insisting on carrying a burden we could set down at any moment? To detest existence and yet to cling to it? In short, to stroke the serpent that's devouring us until he's eaten our very heart?"

"In the various countries I've been fated to cross, and the many inns where I've served, I've noticed an enormous number of people who hated their own existence — and yet I've only ever known eight who actually put an end to their misery: three Black men, four Englishmen, and a German professor named Robeck. I ended up as a servant to the Jew, Don Issachar, who placed me near you, my lovely lady. I've resolved to share your fate, and I've been far more moved by your misfortunes than by my own. I wouldn't have ever mentioned my own troubles if you hadn't provoked me a little, and if it weren't customary to tell stories aboard a ship to kill time. In short, Miss Cunegonde, I have experience, I know the world. So my advice is: amuse yourself, and get each passenger to tell his story. And if there's even one among them who hasn't cursed his life many times, who hasn't often considered himself the unhappiest of mortals, then I give you permission to throw me headfirst into the sea."

chapters.title: Chapter 13 — How Candide Was Forced Away from His Fair Cunegonde and the Old Woman
paragraphs: Having heard the Old Woman's story, the beautiful Cunegonde paid her every courtesy owed to a person of her rank and merit. She also took up her suggestion and got each passenger, one after another, to tell the tale of his adventures. Afterward both she and Candide had to admit that the old woman had been right.

"It's a great pity," said Candide, "that the wise Pangloss was hanged — contrary to normal custom — at an auto-da-fé. He would be able to tell us extraordinary things about the physical and moral evils that blanket the land and sea, and I would feel able, with all due respect, to raise a few objections."

While each passenger was telling his story, the ship made its way. They landed at Buenos Aires. Cunegonde, Captain Candide, and the Old Woman called on the Governor, Don Fernando d'Ibarra y Figueroa y Mascarenes y Lampourdos y Souza. This nobleman had an air of self-importance fitting for a man with so many names. He spoke to people with such noble contempt, held his nose so high, raised his voice so mercilessly, put on such an imperious air, and strutted with such unbearable pride, that anyone greeting him was strongly tempted to give him a sound thrashing. Cunegonde struck him as the most beautiful woman he'd ever seen. The first thing he did was ask whether she wasn't the captain's wife. The way he asked it alarmed Candide: he didn't dare say she was his wife, because she wasn't; and he didn't dare say she was his sister, because she wasn't that either; and although this convenient lie had once been quite fashionable among the ancients, and might have been useful to the moderns, his soul was too pure to betray the truth.
"Miss Cunegonde," he said, "is going to do me the honor of marrying me, and we humbly beg your excellency to give his blessing to our marriage."

Don Fernando d'Ibarra y Figueroa y Mascarenes y Lampourdos y Souza, twirling his moustache, smiled mockingly and ordered Captain Candide to go inspect his company. Candide obeyed, and the Governor was left alone with Miss Cunegonde. He declared his passion, insisting he would marry her the next day — in a church if she wished, or otherwise, whichever she preferred. Cunegonde asked for fifteen minutes to think it over, to consult the Old Woman, and to make up her mind.
The Old Woman spoke to Cunegonde like this:

"Miss, you have seventy-two quarterings of nobility — and not a penny to your name. It's now in your power to become the wife of the greatest lord in South America, who has very handsome moustaches. Is it really for you to pride yourself on absolute fidelity? You've been raped by Bulgarians; a Jew and an Inquisitor have enjoyed your favors. Misfortune is excuse enough. I'll admit that if I were in your place, I wouldn't have the slightest scruple about marrying the Governor and making Captain Candide's fortune in the process."
While the Old Woman was speaking with all the prudence that age and experience provide, a small ship entered the harbor. Aboard were an Alcalde and his constables, and here is what had happened.

As the Old Woman had shrewdly guessed, it was a Grey Friar who had stolen Cunegonde's money and jewels in the town of Badajos while she and Candide were fleeing. The Friar tried to sell some of the diamonds to a jeweler, who recognized them as the Grand Inquisitor's. Before being hanged, the Friar confessed to the theft. He described the people and the route they had taken. The flight of Cunegonde and Candide was already known. They had been traced to Cadiz. A ship was immediately sent in pursuit. That ship was now in the harbor of Buenos Aires. Word spread that the Alcalde was about to come ashore, and that he was hunting for the murderers of my lord the Grand Inquisitor. The prudent Old Woman saw at once what had to be done.
"You can't run," she said to Cunegonde, "and you have nothing to fear, since you weren't the one who killed my lord. Besides, the Governor, who loves you, won't let you be mistreated. So stay."
She then ran straight to Candide.
"Flee," she said, "or in an hour you'll be burned alive."
There wasn't a moment to lose. But how could he leave Cunegonde? And where could he possibly take shelter?

chapters.title: Chapter 14 — How Candide and Cacambo Were Received by the Jesuits of Paraguay
paragraphs: Candide had brought with him from Cadiz the sort of valet one often meets on the Spanish coast and in the American colonies. He was a quarter Spaniard, born of a mixed-race mother in Tucumán. He had been, in turn, a choirboy, a sacristan, a sailor, a monk, a peddler, a soldier, and a lackey. His name was Cacambo, and he loved his master because his master was a very good man. He quickly saddled the two Andalusian horses.
"Come on, master, let's take the old woman's advice — let's go, and run without looking back."
Candide wept.
"Oh! My dear Cunegonde! Must I leave you just when the Governor was about to bless our marriage? Cunegonde, taken so far from home — what will become of you?"
"She'll manage as best she can," said Cacambo. "Women are never at a loss — God takes care of them. Let's run."
"Where are you taking me? Where are we going? What are we going to do without Cunegonde?" said Candide.

"By Saint James of Compostela," said Cacambo, "you were about to go and fight against the Jesuits — let's go and fight for them instead. I know the road well. I'll take you to their kingdom, where they'll be delighted to have a captain who knows the Bulgarian drill. You'll make an enormous fortune. If we can't find our fortune in one world, we'll find it in another. It's a great pleasure to see new things and do new things."
"So you've been in Paraguay before?" said Candide.

"Oh, certainly," Cacambo answered. "I was a servant at the College of the Assumption, and I know the way the good Fathers run their government as well as I know the streets of Cadiz. It's an admirable system. The kingdom is more than three hundred leagues across, divided into thirty provinces. There the Fathers own everything, and the people own nothing. It's a masterpiece of reason and justice. For my part, I find nothing more godlike than these Fathers, who here make war on the kings of Spain and Portugal, and in Europe serve as those same kings' confessors; who here kill Spaniards, and in Madrid send them to heaven. I find it delightful. Let's push on. You're going to be the happiest of mortals. What a pleasure it will be for those Fathers to hear that a captain who knows the Bulgarian drill has arrived!"

As soon as they reached the first checkpoint, Cacambo told the advance guard that a captain wished to speak with my lord the Commandant. Word was sent to the main guard, and immediately a Paraguayan officer ran and threw himself at the Commandant's feet to deliver the news. Candide and Cacambo were disarmed, and their two Andalusian horses seized. The strangers were led in between two files of musketeers. The Commandant stood at the far end, wearing his three-cornered hat, his gown tucked up, a sword at his side, and a spontoon in his hand. He made a signal, and at once twenty-four soldiers surrounded the newcomers. A sergeant told them they would have to wait — the Commandant couldn't speak to them, and the reverend Father Provincial did not permit any Spaniard to open his mouth except in his presence, nor to remain more than three hours in the province.
"And where is the reverend Father Provincial?" said Cacambo.
"He's on the parade ground, having just celebrated mass," the sergeant answered, "and you won't be able to kiss his spurs for another three hours."
"Still," said Cacambo, "the captain isn't a Spaniard, he's a German, and he's about to faint from hunger, just like me. Couldn't we have something for breakfast while we wait for his reverence?"
The sergeant immediately went to report what he'd heard to the Commandant.
"God be praised!" said the reverend Commandant. "Since he's a German, I can speak to him. Bring him to my arbor."

Candide was at once led into a beautiful summer-house, decorated with a very pretty colonnade of green and gold marble, and with trellises enclosing parakeets, hummingbirds, fly-birds, guinea-hens, and every other rare species of bird. An excellent breakfast was served up on gold dishes. And while the Paraguayans were eating maize from wooden bowls in the open fields, baking under the sun, the reverend Father Commandant withdrew to his arbor.

He was a very handsome young man, round-faced, pale-skinned but with high color in his cheeks. He had arched brows, a lively eye, red ears, vermilion lips, and a bold bearing — though a boldness that belonged neither to a Spaniard nor a Jesuit. Their weapons were returned to Candide and Cacambo, as were the two Andalusian horses. Cacambo fed them some oats just outside the arbor, keeping an eye on them the whole time in case of a surprise.
Candide first kissed the hem of the Commandant's robe, then they sat down at the table.
"So you are a German?" the Jesuit asked him in that language.
"Yes, reverend Father," Candide answered.
As they spoke these words they looked at each other in enormous astonishment, with an emotion they couldn't hide.
"And what part of Germany are you from?" the Jesuit asked.
"I'm from the filthy province of Westphalia," Candide answered. "I was born in the Castle of Thunder-ten-Tronckh."
"Oh, heavens! Is it possible?" cried the Commandant.
"What a miracle!" cried Candide.
"Is it really you?" said the Commandant.
"It isn't possible!" said Candide.
They stepped back. They embraced. They wept torrents.

"What — is it you, reverend Father? You, the brother of the beautiful Cunegonde! You, whom the Bulgarians were supposed to have killed! You, the Baron's son! You, a Jesuit in Paraguay! I must admit, this is a strange world we live in. Oh, Pangloss! Pangloss! How happy you would be if you hadn't been hanged!"

The Commandant dismissed the Black slaves and the Paraguayans who had been serving them drinks in goblets of rock crystal. He thanked God and Saint Ignatius a thousand times. He clasped Candide in his arms. Their faces were drenched with tears.
"You'll be even more surprised, more moved, more overcome," said Candide, "when I tell you that Cunegonde, your sister, whom you believe was disemboweled, is in perfect health."
"Where?"
"In your neighborhood, with the Governor of Buenos Aires. And I was on my way to fight against you."

Every word they uttered in this long conversation piled wonder on top of wonder. Their souls danced on their tongues, listened at their ears, and sparkled in their eyes. Being Germans, they sat at the table a long while, waiting for the reverend Father Provincial, and the Commandant spoke to his dear Candide as follows.

chapters.title: Chapter 15 — How Candide Killed the Brother of His Dear Cunegonde
paragraphs: "I will always carry with me the memory of that horrible day when I saw my father and mother killed and my sister raped. When the Bulgarians withdrew, we couldn't find my dear sister. But my mother, my father, and I, along with two maidservants and three little boys — all of them slain — were loaded onto a hearse to be taken for burial at a Jesuit chapel about two leagues from our family estate. A Jesuit sprinkled us with holy water. It was horribly salty. A few drops landed in my eyes. The father noticed that my eyelids twitched a little. He put his hand on my heart and felt it beating. I was given medical help, and within three weeks I had recovered. You know, my dear Candide, I was very good-looking. I grew much better-looking still, and the reverend Father Didrie, Superior of that house, conceived the tenderest affection for me. He gave me the habit of the order, and a few years later I was sent to Rome. The Father-General needed fresh recruits of young German Jesuits. The rulers of Paraguay accept as few Spanish Jesuits as possible — they prefer those of other nationalities, as more obedient to their commands. The reverend Father-General judged me fit to come work in this vineyard. Three of us set out — a Pole, a Tyrolean, and myself. On arrival I was honored with a sub-deaconship and a lieutenancy. Today I am both colonel and priest. We'll give the King of Spain's troops a warm reception; I guarantee they'll be excommunicated and thoroughly beaten. Providence is sending you here to help us. But is it really true that my dear sister Cunegonde is in the area, with the Governor of Buenos Aires?"
Candide swore on oath that nothing could be more true, and their tears started up again.
The Baron couldn't stop embracing Candide. He called him his brother, his savior.
"Ah! Perhaps," he said, "we'll enter the town together as conquerors, my dear Candide, and recover my sister Cunegonde."
"That's all I want," said Candide, "because I intended to marry her, and I still hope to."

"You insolent wretch!" replied the Baron. "Would you have the gall to marry my sister, who has seventy-two quarterings of nobility? I find you have the most astonishing nerve to even mention such a presumptuous plan!"
Candide, thunderstruck by this speech, replied:

"Reverend Father, all the quarterings in the world mean nothing. I rescued your sister from the arms of a Jew and an Inquisitor. She owes me a great deal. She wishes to marry me. Master Pangloss always told me all men are equal, and I will certainly marry her."

"We'll see about that, you scoundrel!" said the Jesuit Baron de Thunder-ten-Tronckh, and at that moment struck him across the face with the flat of his sword. In an instant Candide drew his rapier and plunged it up to the hilt into the Jesuit's belly. But as he pulled it out, steaming hot, he burst into tears.

"Good God!" he said. "I've killed my old master, my friend, my brother-in-law! I'm the most good-natured creature in the world, and yet I've already killed three men — and two of the three were priests."
Cacambo, who was standing sentry at the door of the arbor, ran in.
"There's nothing left to do but sell our lives as dearly as we can," his master said to him. "No doubt someone will come into the arbor any minute, and we'll have to die sword in hand."

Cacambo, who had been in many scrapes in his life, kept his head. He pulled off the Baron's Jesuit habit, dressed Candide in it, handed him the square cap, and got him into the saddle. All of this was done in the blink of an eye.
"Let's gallop fast, master. Everyone will take you for a Jesuit off to give orders to his troops, and we'll have crossed the frontier before they can catch up."
He was already flying as he said these words, shouting out loud in Spanish:
"Make way, make way, for the reverend Father Colonel."

chapters.title: Chapter 16 — Adventures of the Two Travellers, with Two Girls, Two Monkeys, and the Savages Called Oreillons
paragraphs: Candide and his valet had passed the checkpoint before anyone in the camp even knew the German Jesuit was dead. The cautious Cacambo had taken care to stuff his bag with bread, chocolate, bacon, fruit, and a few bottles of wine. On their Andalusian horses they pushed on into an unknown country, where they could find no trodden path. At last they came upon a beautiful meadow crossed by bubbling streams. Here the two adventurers let their horses graze. Cacambo suggested to his master that they eat something, and set the example himself.

"How can you ask me to eat ham," said Candide, "after killing the Baron's son, and being doomed never to see the beautiful Cunegonde again? What good does it do me to drag out my miserable days, far from her, in remorse and despair? And what is the Journal of Trévoux going to say?"

Even as he lamented his fate, he went on eating. The sun went down. The two wanderers heard some small cries that seemed to be coming from women. They couldn't tell whether they were cries of pain or of joy, but they sprang up instantly with that uneasy alarm that every little sound inspires in unknown country. The noise was coming from two naked girls, who were running across the meadow with two monkeys chasing them and biting their buttocks. Candide was moved with pity. He had learned to fire a musket in the Bulgarian service, and he was so skilled at it that he could hit a hazelnut in a hedge without touching a single leaf on the tree. He picked up his double-barreled Spanish musket, fired, and killed both monkeys.

"God be praised! My dear Cacambo, I've rescued those two poor creatures from a terrible danger. If I committed a sin killing an Inquisitor and a Jesuit, I've now more than made up for it by saving these girls' lives. Perhaps they're young ladies of noble family, and this adventure might earn us great advantages in this country."
He was about to continue, but stopped short when he saw the two girls tenderly embracing the monkeys, weeping over their bodies, and filling the air with the most desolate lamentations.
"I hardly expected to see such tender feelings," he finally said to Cacambo. Cacambo answered:
"Master, that's a fine thing you've done now — you've just killed those two young ladies' lovers."
"Their lovers! Is it possible? You're joking, Cacambo, I can never believe it!"

"Dear master," replied Cacambo, "you are always surprised by everything. Why should it seem so strange that in some countries there are monkeys who work their way into the affections of the ladies? They are a quarter human, just as I am a quarter Spaniard."

"Alas!" Candide replied, "I remember Master Pangloss telling me that in former times such things did happen — that these mixed couplings produced Centaurs, Fauns, and Satyrs, and that many ancients had seen such creatures. But I took the whole thing for a fable."

"You ought to be convinced now," said Cacambo, "that it's the plain truth, and you can see what use people who haven't had a proper education make of those creatures. My only fear is that those ladies will play some nasty trick on us."

These sensible reflections persuaded Candide to leave the meadow and plunge into a forest. He had supper there with Cacambo, and after cursing the Portuguese Inquisitor, the Governor of Buenos Aires, and the Baron, they fell asleep on the moss. When they woke up, they found they couldn't move. During the night the Oreillons, the natives of that country — to whom the girls had denounced them — had bound them with cords made of tree bark. They were surrounded by fifty naked Oreillons armed with bows and arrows, with clubs and stone hatchets. Some were bringing a great cauldron to a boil, others were preparing spits, and all of them were shouting:
"A Jesuit! A Jesuit! We'll have our revenge, we'll have an excellent meal — let's eat the Jesuit, let's eat him up!"
"I told you, my dear master," cried Cacambo miserably, "that those two girls were going to play us a nasty trick."
Candide, seeing the cauldron and the spits, cried out:

"We are certainly going to be either roasted or boiled. Ah! What would Master Pangloss say if he could see what pure nature actually produces? Everything may be for the best, but I must say it's a hard thing to have lost Miss Cunegonde and now to be put on a spit by Oreillons."
Cacambo never lost his head.
"Don't despair," he said to the miserable Candide. "I understand a bit of these people's jargon — I'll speak to them."
"Be sure," said Candide, "to explain to them how horrifyingly inhuman it is to cook men, and how very un-Christian."

"Gentlemen," said Cacambo, "you're counting on dining on a Jesuit today. That's fine — nothing's more fair than to treat your enemies that way. In fact, the law of nature teaches us to kill our neighbor, and that's the practice the world over. We don't eat them ourselves because we have better food available; but you don't have the same resources, and it's certainly better to devour your enemies than to abandon the fruits of your victory to the crows and ravens. But gentlemen, surely you wouldn't want to eat your friends. You believe you're about to spit a Jesuit, but in fact he is your defender. It's the enemy of your enemies that you're about to roast. As for me, I was born in your country. This gentleman is my master, and far from being a Jesuit, he has just killed one, and is now wearing his clothing — that's where your mistake comes from. To prove to you that I'm telling the truth, take this habit and carry it to the first border post of the Jesuit kingdom, and ask whether my master didn't just kill a Jesuit officer. It won't take you long, and you can always eat us if you find I've lied to you. But I've told you the truth. You're too well-versed in the principles of international law, humanity, and justice not to pardon us."

The Oreillons thought this speech very reasonable. They dispatched two of their leading men with all urgency to investigate the matter. The envoys carried out their commission like men of sense and soon returned with good news. The Oreillons untied their prisoners, showed them every courtesy, offered them girls, gave them refreshments, and escorted them back to the edge of their territory, crying out in great joy:
"He's no Jesuit! He's no Jesuit!"
Candide couldn't help being amazed at the cause of his own rescue.

"What a people!" he said. "What men! What customs! If I hadn't been lucky enough to run Miss Cunegonde's brother through the body, I would have been devoured without hope of rescue. But all things considered, pure nature is good — since these people, instead of feasting on my flesh, have shown me a thousand courtesies the moment they realized I wasn't a Jesuit."

chapters.title: Chapter 17 — Arrival of Candide and His Valet at El Dorado, and What They Saw There
paragraphs: "You see," said Cacambo to Candide as soon as they reached the borders of the Oreillons' country, "this hemisphere is no better than the others, take my word for it. Let's head back to Europe by the shortest route."

"Go back how?" said Candide. "And where would we go? To my own country? The Bulgarians and Abares are slaughtering everyone. To Portugal? I'll be burned there. And if we stay here, we're at risk every moment of being put on a spit. But how can I bring myself to leave the part of the world where my dear Cunegonde lives?"
"Let's head toward Cayenne," said Cacambo. "We'll find Frenchmen there — they wander all over the world. They may be able to help us. God may yet take pity on us."

Getting to Cayenne wasn't easy. They knew roughly which direction to go in, but rivers, cliffs, bandits, and savages blocked them at every turn. Their horses died of exhaustion. Their provisions ran out. For a whole month they lived on wild fruit, and at last found themselves near a little river bordered with coconut palms, which sustained both their lives and their hopes.
Cacambo, who gave as good advice as the Old Woman, said to Candide:

"We can't hold out any longer. We've walked enough. I see an empty canoe by the riverbank — let's fill it with coconuts, throw ourselves in, and let the current take us. A river always leads somewhere inhabited. If we don't find anything pleasant, we'll at least find something new."
"With all my heart," said Candide. "Let's commit ourselves to Providence."

They drifted a few leagues between banks that were sometimes flowering, sometimes barren — in some places smooth, in others jagged. The stream kept widening until at last it vanished under an arch of terrifying rocks that soared up to the sky. The two travelers had the courage to entrust themselves to the current. Where the river suddenly narrowed, it hurled them along with a dreadful noise and speed. At the end of twenty-four hours they saw daylight again, but their canoe was smashed to pieces against the rocks. For a league they had to crawl from rock to rock, until at last they discovered a wide plain bounded by inaccessible mountains. The country was cultivated as much for pleasure as for need. Everywhere, the useful was also the beautiful. The roads were covered — or rather adorned — with carriages of glittering shape and material, carrying men and women of astonishing beauty, drawn by large red sheep that outran the finest coursers of Andalusia, Tetuán, and Meknes.
"Well," said Candide, "here at last is a country that beats Westphalia."

He and Cacambo got out near the first village they saw. On the outskirts some children dressed in tattered brocades were playing quoits. Our travelers from the other world entertained themselves by watching. The quoits were large round disks — yellow, red, and green — that shone with an extraordinary luster.
