The travelers picked a few up off the ground. One was gold, another emerald, another ruby — the smallest of them would have been the greatest jewel in the Mogul's throne.
"No doubt," said Cacambo, "these children playing quoits must be the king's sons."
The village schoolmaster appeared at that moment and called them in to class.
"That must be," said Candide, "the tutor to the royal family."

The little truants dropped their game immediately, leaving the quoits on the ground along with all their other toys. Candide picked them up, ran after the master, and presented them to him in the most humble fashion, making signs to indicate that their royal highnesses had forgotten their gold and jewels. The schoolmaster, smiling, tossed them back on the ground, then — looking at Candide in considerable surprise — went on about his business.
The travelers, however, made sure to pocket the gold, the rubies, and the emeralds.
"Where are we?" cried Candide. "The king's children in this country must be well brought up, since they're taught to despise gold and precious stones."

Cacambo was as surprised as Candide. Eventually they reached the first house in the village. It was built like a European palace. A crowd pressed around the door, and there were even more people inside. They heard the most pleasant music, and became aware of a delicious cooking smell. Cacambo went up to the door and heard people speaking Peruvian — it was his mother tongue, since, as is well known, Cacambo was born in Tucumán, in a village where no other language was spoken.
"I'll be your interpreter here," he said to Candide. "Let's go in — it's a public inn."

At once two waiters and two girls, dressed in cloth of gold with their hair tied up in ribbons, invited them to sit down at the landlord's table. They were served four bowls of soup, each garnished with two young parrots; a boiled condor that weighed two hundred pounds; two roasted monkeys, of exquisite flavor; three hundred hummingbirds on one platter, and six hundred fly-birds on another; exquisite ragouts; delicious pastries — all served up on dishes of a kind of rock crystal. The waiters and girls poured out several liqueurs distilled from sugar cane.
Most of the customers were traders and wagoners, all extremely polite. They asked Cacambo a few questions with great tact, and answered his with the most obliging manner.

As soon as dinner was over, Cacambo, like Candide, thought they could settle their bill by laying down two of those big gold pieces they'd picked up. The landlord and landlady burst out laughing and held their sides. When the fit passed:

"Gentlemen," said the landlord, "it's obvious you're strangers — and we're not used to entertaining such guests. Forgive us for laughing when you offered us the pebbles from our highways in payment of your bill. No doubt you don't have the currency of the country — but you don't need any money at all to dine in this house. All inns established for the convenience of commerce are paid for by the government. You've fared only modestly because this is a poor village; but everywhere else, you'll be received as you deserve."
Cacambo translated the whole speech to Candide with great astonishment, and Candide was equally astonished to hear it.

"What sort of country is this," they said to each other, "a country unknown to the rest of the world, where nature is of a kind entirely different from ours? This must be the country where everything is well — for there absolutely has to be one such place. And whatever Master Pangloss used to say, I often found that things went very badly in Westphalia."

chapters.title: Chapter 18 — What They Saw in the Country of El Dorado
paragraphs: Cacambo expressed his curiosity to the landlord, who replied:
"I'm very ignorant, and none the worse for it. But we have here in the neighborhood an old man retired from the Court, the most learned and most open-tongued man in the kingdom."

He took Cacambo at once to the old man. Candide now played only a secondary role, and accompanied his valet. They entered a very simple house — the door was merely silver, the ceilings merely gold, but wrought in such elegant taste as to rival the richest. The antechamber was admittedly only encrusted with rubies and emeralds, but the order in which everything was arranged more than made up for this great simplicity.

The old man received the strangers on his sofa, which was stuffed with hummingbird feathers, and ordered his servants to present them with liqueurs in diamond goblets. After which he satisfied their curiosity in the following terms:

"I am now one hundred and seventy-two years old, and I learned from my late father, Master of the Horse to the King, the amazing revolutions of Peru, of which he had been an eyewitness. The kingdom we now live in is the ancient country of the Incas, who left it very imprudently to conquer another part of the world, and were in the end destroyed by the Spaniards."

"The princes of their family who stayed behind in their native land were far wiser. With the whole nation's consent, they decreed that no inhabitant should ever be allowed to leave this little kingdom — and that's what has preserved our innocence and happiness. The Spaniards had a vague notion of this country and called it El Dorado; and an Englishman named Sir Walter Raleigh came close to it about a hundred years ago. But since we are surrounded by impassable cliffs and precipices, we have so far been sheltered from the rapacity of the European nations, who have an inconceivable lust for the pebbles and dirt of our country, for which they would murder every last one of us."

The conversation was long: it turned chiefly on their form of government, their customs, their women, their public entertainments, and the arts. Finally Candide, who had always had a taste for metaphysics, got Cacambo to ask whether there was any religion in the country.
The old man colored a little.
"How," he said, "can you even doubt it? Do you take us for ungrateful wretches?"
Cacambo humbly asked what the religion of El Dorado was.
The old man colored again.
"Can there be two religions?" he said. "We have, I believe, the religion of the whole world: we worship God night and morning."
"Do you worship only one God?" said Cacambo, still acting as interpreter for Candide's doubts.
"Of course," said the old man, "there aren't two, or three, or four. I must confess the people from your side of the world ask very extraordinary questions."
Candide wasn't tired of cross-examining the good old man yet — he wanted to know how they prayed to God in El Dorado.
"We don't pray to him," said the worthy sage. "We have nothing to ask of him. He has given us everything we need, and we return him thanks unceasingly."
Candide, being curious to see the priests, asked where they were. The good old man smiled.
"My friend," he said, "we are all priests. The King and all the heads of households sing solemn hymns of thanksgiving every morning, accompanied by five or six thousand musicians."
"What! You have no monks who teach, who argue, who govern, who scheme, and who burn anyone who disagrees with them?"
"We would have to be mad indeed if that were the case," said the old man. "Here we are all of one opinion, and we have no idea what you mean by monks."
Throughout all this Candide was in raptures, and he said to himself:

"This is vastly different from Westphalia and the Baron's castle. If our friend Pangloss had seen El Dorado, he would no longer have said that the castle of Thunder-ten-Tronckh was the finest thing on earth. It's clear one must travel."
After this long conversation, the old man ordered a coach and six sheep readied, and assigned twelve of his servants to escort the travelers to Court.

"Excuse me," he said, "if my age deprives me of the honor of accompanying you. The King will receive you in a way that can't fail to please you; and no doubt you'll make allowances for the customs of the country, should anything not be quite to your taste."

Candide and Cacambo got into the coach. The six sheep flew, and in less than four hours they reached the King's palace, situated at the far end of the capital. The main gate was two hundred and twenty feet high and one hundred wide. Words fail to describe the materials it was built of. It's plain such materials must be enormously superior to those pebbles and sand we call gold and precious stones.

Twenty beautiful damsels of the King's guard received Candide and Cacambo as they stepped down from the coach, escorted them to the bath, and dressed them in robes woven from hummingbird down. After which the high crown officers, of both sexes, led them to the King's apartment between two files of a thousand musicians on each side. As they approached the audience chamber Cacambo asked one of the great officers how to pay his respects to His Majesty — whether they should throw themselves on their knees or on their bellies, whether they should put their hands on their heads or behind their backs, whether they should lick the dust off the floor — in short, what was the ceremony?
"The custom," said the great officer, "is to embrace the King and kiss him on each cheek."
Candide and Cacambo threw themselves around His Majesty's neck. He received them with all the kindness imaginable, and politely invited them to supper.

While they waited, they were shown the city — the public buildings raised as high as the clouds, the marketplaces adorned with a thousand columns, the fountains of spring water, the fountains of rosewater, the fountains of sugar-cane liqueur constantly flowing into great squares paved with a kind of precious stone that gave off a delicious fragrance like cloves and cinnamon. Candide asked to see the court of justice, the parliament. He was told they had none, and that they knew nothing of lawsuits. He asked if they had prisons. No, he was told. But what surprised him most, and gave him the greatest pleasure, was the palace of sciences, where he saw a gallery two thousand feet long, filled with instruments used in mathematics and physics.

After rambling about the city all afternoon and seeing only a thousandth part of it, they were brought back to the royal palace, where Candide sat down at table with His Majesty, his valet Cacambo, and several ladies. Never was there better entertainment, and never was more wit displayed at a table than that which fell from His Majesty's lips. Cacambo translated the King's witticisms to Candide, and even in translation they still came across as witticisms. Of all the things that astonished Candide, this was not the least.
They spent a month in this hospitable place. Candide kept saying to Cacambo:

"I admit once again, my friend, that the castle I was born in is nothing compared to this. But after all, Miss Cunegonde isn't here, and you, no doubt, have some mistress in Europe. If we stay, we'll only be on the same footing as everyone else — whereas if we return to our old world with just twelve sheep loaded with El Dorado pebbles, we'll be richer than all the kings of Europe put together. We'll have no more Inquisitors to fear, and we can easily recover Miss Cunegonde."

This speech appealed to Cacambo. Human beings are so fond of wandering, of cutting a figure back home, and of boasting about what they've seen in their travels, that the two happy ones decided to stop being happy, and to ask His Majesty for permission to leave.

"You're being foolish," said the King. "I know my kingdom is a small place, but when a person is comfortably settled somewhere, he should stay there. I have no right to detain strangers. That would be a tyranny neither our customs nor our laws permit. All men are free. Go when you wish — but leaving will be very difficult. It's impossible to go up that rapid river on which you came down as by a miracle, and which runs under vaulted rocks. The mountains surrounding my kingdom are ten thousand feet high and as steep as walls. Each is more than ten leagues across, and there's no way down them but over precipices. Still, since you absolutely insist on leaving, I'll order my engineers to build a machine that can carry you down safely. Once we've conducted you over the mountains, no one can accompany you any further — my subjects have sworn never to leave the kingdom, and they are too wise to break their vow. Ask me for anything else you please."
"We want nothing from Your Majesty," said Candide, "but a few sheep loaded with provisions, pebbles, and the dirt of this country."
The King laughed.
"I can't imagine," he said, "what pleasure you Europeans find in our yellow clay, but take as much as you like — and much good may it do you."

He at once instructed his engineers to build a machine to hoist these two extraordinary men out of the kingdom. Three thousand good mathematicians went to work. It was ready in fifteen days, and cost no more than twenty million sterling in the local currency. Candide and Cacambo were placed on the machine. There were two great red sheep saddled and bridled for them to ride once they were beyond the mountains, twenty pack-sheep loaded with provisions, thirty carrying gifts of the country's curiosities, and fifty loaded with gold, diamonds, and precious stones. The King embraced the two wanderers very tenderly.

Their departure, and the ingenious way in which they and their sheep were hoisted over the mountains, was a splendid spectacle. The mathematicians said their goodbyes after conveying them to a place of safety, and Candide had no other desire, no other aim, than to present his sheep to Miss Cunegonde.
"Now," he said, "we can pay the Governor of Buenos Aires, if Miss Cunegonde can be ransomed. Let's make for Cayenne. Let's take ship, and afterwards we'll see which kingdom we can afford to buy."

chapters.title: Chapter 19 — What Happened to Them at Surinam and How Candide Got Acquainted with Martin
paragraphs: Our travelers spent the first day very pleasantly. They were delighted to possess more treasure than all of Asia, Europe, and Africa could scrape together. Candide, in his rapture, carved Cunegonde's name into the trees. On the second day, two of their sheep plunged into a swamp, where they and their cargo were lost. Two more died of exhaustion a few days later. Seven or eight perished from hunger in a desert, and still others later fell from precipices. At last, after a hundred days of travel, only two sheep remained. Candide said to Cacambo:
"My friend, you see how perishable the riches of this world are. Nothing is solid except virtue, and the happiness of seeing Cunegonde again."

"I agree with everything you say," said Cacambo, "but we still have two sheep left, with more treasure than the King of Spain will ever own. And I see a town over there which I believe is Surinam, which belongs to the Dutch. We're at the end of all our troubles, and at the beginning of happiness."
As they drew near the town, they saw a Black man stretched on the ground, wearing only half his clothes — that is, his blue linen drawers. The poor man had lost his left leg and his right hand.
"Good God!" said Candide in Dutch, "what are you doing there, friend, in such a shocking state?"
"I am waiting for my master, Mynheer Vanderdendur, the famous merchant," the man answered.
"Was it Mynheer Vanderdendur," said Candide, "who treated you like this?"

"Yes, sir," the man answered. "That's the custom. They give us a pair of linen drawers as our only garment twice a year. When we work at the sugar canes, and the mill catches hold of a finger, they cut off the hand. When we try to run away, they cut off the leg. Both have happened to me. That's the price at which you eat sugar in Europe. And yet when my mother sold me for ten patagons on the Guinea coast, she said to me: 'My dear child, bless our fetishes, worship them forever, they'll make your life happy. You have the honor of being the slave of our lords, the whites, which is making your father and mother's fortune.' Alas! I don't know whether I've made their fortune, but I do know they haven't made mine. Dogs, monkeys, and parrots are a thousand times less miserable than I am. The Dutch fetishes who converted me declare every Sunday that we are all children of Adam — Blacks as well as whites. I'm no genealogist, but if those preachers are telling the truth, then we're all second cousins. And you have to admit, there's no more barbaric way to treat your relatives."
"Oh, Pangloss!" cried Candide. "You hadn't guessed at this abomination. This is the end. I'll have to renounce your optimism at last."
"What is this optimism?" asked Cacambo.
"Alas," said Candide, "it's the madness of insisting that everything is well when it is wrong."
Looking at the man, he shed tears, and weeping, he entered Surinam.

The first thing they asked about was whether there was a ship in port that could be sent to Buenos Aires. The man they consulted was a Spanish sea-captain who offered to come to reasonable terms with them. He arranged to meet them at an inn, where Candide and the faithful Cacambo went with their two sheep, and waited for him.
Candide, whose heart was always on his lips, told the Spaniard all his adventures, and confessed that he intended to elope with Miss Cunegonde.
"Then I'll take very good care not to carry you to Buenos Aires," said the captain. "I'd be hanged, and so would you. The beautiful Cunegonde is my lord's favorite mistress."
This was a thunderclap for Candide. He wept a long while. At last he drew Cacambo aside.

"Here, my dear friend," he said, "this is what you must do. Each of us has five or six millions in diamonds in our pockets. You're shrewder than I am — you must go to Buenos Aires and fetch Miss Cunegonde. If the Governor makes any trouble, give him a million; if he won't give her up, give him two. Since you haven't killed an Inquisitor, no one will suspect you. I'll get another ship and go wait for you in Venice. It's a free country, where there's no danger from Bulgarians, Abares, Jews, or Inquisitors."

Cacambo applauded this wise plan. He was heartbroken at parting from so good a master, who had become his close friend; but the pleasure of serving him won out over the pain of leaving him. They embraced in tears. Candide charged him not to forget the good Old Woman. Cacambo set out that very day. This Cacambo was a very honest fellow.

Candide stayed on in Surinam a while longer, waiting for another captain to carry him and the two remaining sheep to Italy. After he had hired servants and bought everything necessary for a long voyage, Mynheer Vanderdendur, captain of a large vessel, came and offered his services.
"How much will you charge," Candide asked him, "to carry me directly to Venice — me, my servants, my baggage, and these two sheep?"
The skipper asked ten thousand piastres. Candide didn't hesitate.
"Oh! Oh!" the shrewd Vanderdendur said to himself. "This stranger pays ten thousand piastres without blinking! He must be very rich."
Returning a moment later, he let him know that on further reflection, he couldn't undertake the voyage for less than twenty thousand piastres.
"Very well, you shall have them," said Candide.
"Aha!" the skipper said to himself, "this man agrees to twenty thousand piastres as easily as he did to ten."
He came back again and declared that he couldn't carry him to Venice for less than thirty thousand piastres.
"Then you shall have thirty thousand," replied Candide.

"Oh! Oh!" the Dutch skipper said to himself once more. "Thirty thousand piastres are a trifle to this man. Surely these sheep must be loaded with an immense treasure. Let's say no more about it. First let him pay out the thirty thousand piastres, then we'll see."

Candide sold two small diamonds, the smaller of which was worth more than all the skipper was asking for the passage. He paid him in advance. The two sheep were brought on board. Candide followed in a small boat to meet the ship in the roads. The skipper saw his chance, set sail, and put out to sea with the wind favoring him. Stunned and dazed, Candide soon lost sight of the ship.
"Alas!" he said, "this is a trick worthy of the old world!"

He put back to shore, overwhelmed with grief — for he'd lost enough to make the fortune of twenty monarchs. He called on the Dutch magistrate, and in his distress he knocked loudly at the door. He went in and told his story, raising his voice with unnecessary force. The magistrate began by fining him ten thousand piastres for making a disturbance. Then he listened patiently, promised to look into the matter when the skipper returned, and ordered him to pay another ten thousand piastres for the cost of the hearing.

This drove Candide to despair. He had, in truth, endured misfortunes a thousand times worse — but the coolness of the magistrate, and of the skipper who had robbed him, stoked his rage and plunged him into a deep melancholy. The villainy of humankind rose up before him in all its ugliness, and his mind filled with dark thoughts. At last, hearing that a French ship was ready to set sail for Bordeaux — and since he no longer had sheep loaded with diamonds to bring along — he booked a cabin at the usual price. He let it be known in the town that he would pay passage and board and give two thousand piastres to any honest man who would make the voyage with him, on condition that the man was the most dissatisfied with his own situation and the unhappiest in the whole province.

Such a crowd of candidates turned up that a whole fleet of ships could scarcely have held them. Wanting to choose from the best, Candide picked out about a twentieth of them who seemed sociable, and who all claimed to deserve his preference. He assembled them at his inn and gave them a supper on condition that each took an oath to tell his story truthfully, with the promise that he would pick the one who seemed most justly discontented with his situation, and give the others some consolation.

They sat until four in the morning. As Candide listened to their adventures, he was reminded of what the Old Woman had told him on their voyage to Buenos Aires, and of her bet that there wasn't a single person on board the ship who hadn't suffered enormous misfortunes. He thought of Pangloss at every story he heard.
"This Pangloss," he said, "would have a hard time defending his system. I wish he were here. Certainly, if all is for the best, it's in El Dorado and not in the rest of the world."
At last he chose a poor man of letters, who had worked for ten years for the booksellers of Amsterdam. He judged that there wasn't a trade in the whole world more likely to disgust a man.

This philosopher was an honest fellow — but he had been robbed by his wife, beaten by his son, and abandoned by his daughter, who'd run off with a Portuguese. He had just been deprived of a small government post that had been his livelihood, and he was being persecuted by the preachers of Surinam, who took him for a Socinian. It has to be admitted that the others were at least as miserable as he was — but Candide hoped the philosopher would entertain him during the voyage. All the other candidates complained that Candide had done them a great injustice, but he calmed them by giving each of them a hundred piastres.

chapters.title: Chapter 20 — What Happened at Sea to Candide and Martin
paragraphs: The old philosopher, whose name was Martin, set sail with Candide for Bordeaux. They had both seen and suffered a great deal; and if the ship had been bound from Surinam to Japan by way of the Cape of Good Hope, the subject of moral and physical evil alone would have kept them entertained for the whole voyage.

Candide, however, had one great advantage over Martin: he still hoped to see Miss Cunegonde, whereas Martin had nothing to hope for at all. Besides, Candide had money and jewels, and although he had lost a hundred large red sheep loaded with the greatest treasure on earth, and although the Dutch skipper's swindle still weighed heavily on his mind, still, when he thought about what he had left, and when he mentioned Cunegonde's name — especially toward the end of a meal — he leaned toward Pangloss's doctrine.
"But you, Mr. Martin," he said to the philosopher, "what do you make of all this? What are your thoughts on moral and physical evil?"
"Sir," answered Martin, "our priests accused me of being a Socinian, but the truth is I'm a Manichean."
"You're joking," said Candide. "There are no Manicheans left in the world."
"There's one," said Martin. "I can't help it. I don't know how to think otherwise."
"You must be possessed by the devil," said Candide.

"He's so deeply involved in the affairs of this world," Martin answered, "that he might very well be in me, just as he's in everyone else. But I'll admit that when I cast an eye on this globe — or rather, on this little ball — I can't help thinking God has abandoned it to some malevolent being. I except El Dorado, always. I've hardly ever known a city that didn't want to see a neighboring city destroyed, or a family that didn't wish to wipe out some other family. Everywhere, the weak curse the powerful they cringe before, and the powerful beat them like sheep whose wool and flesh they sell. A million regimented assassins, from one end of Europe to the other, earn their bread by disciplined robbery and murder, for want of a more honest living. Even in cities that seem to enjoy peace, where the arts flourish, the inhabitants are devoured by more envy, worry, and unease than anyone in a besieged town. Private griefs are crueler than public calamities. In short, I've seen so much and suffered so much that I'm a Manichean."
"Still, there are some good things," said Candide.
"There may be," said Martin, "but I don't know them."

In the middle of this argument they heard the report of cannon. It redoubled every instant. Each pulled out his telescope. They saw two ships in close combat about three miles off. The wind brought both so near the French vessel that our travelers had the pleasure of watching the fight at their leisure. At last one let off a broadside, aimed so low and so true that the other sank straight to the bottom. Candide and Martin could clearly see a hundred men on the deck of the sinking ship; they raised their hands to heaven and let out terrible cries, and the next moment were swallowed up by the sea.
"Well," said Martin, "this is how men treat each other."
"True," said Candide. "There's something diabolical in this business."

As he spoke, he saw something shining red swimming close to the ship — he couldn't tell what. They lowered the longboat to investigate: it was one of his sheep! Candide was more overjoyed at finding this one sheep than he had been grieved at the loss of the hundred laden with the great diamonds of El Dorado.

The French captain soon realized that the captain of the victorious ship was a Spaniard, and that the other was a Dutch pirate — the very same one who had robbed Candide. The immense plunder this villain had amassed went down into the sea with him, and of all of it only one sheep was saved.
"You see," said Candide to Martin, "that crime is sometimes punished. This rogue of a Dutch skipper met the fate he deserved."
"Yes," said Martin, "but why should the passengers be destroyed along with him? God has punished the swindler, and the devil has drowned the rest."

The French and Spanish ships continued on their course, and Candide continued his conversation with Martin. They argued for fifteen days in a row, and on the last of those fifteen days they were exactly where they'd been on the first. But still they chatted, they traded ideas, they consoled each other. Candide stroked his sheep.
"Since I've found you again," he said, "I may yet find my Cunegonde too."

chapters.title: Chapter 21 — Candide and Martin, Reasoning, Draw Near the Coast of France
paragraphs: At last they sighted the coast of France.
"Have you ever been to France, Mr. Martin?" asked Candide.

"Yes," said Martin, "I've traveled through several of its provinces. In some, half the people are fools; in others, they're too clever by half. In some they're weak and simple; in others, they pretend to be witty. In all of them, the main occupation is love, the next is slander, and the third is talking nonsense."
"But, Mr. Martin, have you seen Paris?"

"Yes, I have. You find every one of those types there. It's chaos—a confused crowd where everyone chases pleasure and hardly anyone finds it, at least as far as I could tell. I didn't stay long. The moment I arrived, pickpockets at the fair of Saint-Germain robbed me of everything I had. I was then mistaken for a thief myself and spent eight days in prison. After that, I worked as a proofreader to earn enough money to walk back to Holland. I got to know the whole hack-writing rabble, the partisan rabble, and the fanatical rabble. They say there are some very polite people in that city, and I'd like to believe it."

"For my part, I have no desire to see France," said Candide. "You can imagine that after spending a month in El Dorado, there's nothing left on earth I want to see except Miss Cunegonde. I'm going to wait for her in Venice. We'll pass through France on our way to Italy. Will you come with me?"

"Gladly," said Martin. "They say Venice is only good for its own nobility, but that foreigners get a warm welcome if they have plenty of money. I have none; you have plenty, so I'll follow you to the ends of the earth."
"But do you believe," said Candide, "that the earth was originally a sea, as that big book belonging to the captain claims?"
"I don't believe a word of it," said Martin, "any more than I believe the many other nonsensical ideas that have been published lately."
"Then for what purpose was this world made?" said Candide.
"To torment us," answered Martin.
"Aren't you utterly astonished," Candide went on, "at the love those two girls of the Oreillons had for those monkeys—the story I told you about?"
"Not at all," said Martin. "I don't see anything strange about that passion. I've seen so many extraordinary things that I've stopped being surprised by any of them."

"Do you believe," said Candide, "that men have always slaughtered each other the way they do today—that they have always been liars, cheats, traitors, ingrates, brigands, idiots, thieves, scoundrels, gluttons, drunkards, misers, envious, ambitious, bloodthirsty, slanderers, debauchees, fanatics, hypocrites, and fools?"
"Do you believe," said Martin, "that hawks have always eaten pigeons whenever they caught them?"
"Yes, without a doubt," said Candide.
"Well then," said Martin, "if hawks have always had the same character, why do you imagine that men might have changed theirs?"
"Oh!" said Candide, "there's a vast difference, because free will——"
And reasoning like this, they arrived at Bordeaux.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 — What Happened in France to Candide and Martin
paragraphs: Candide stayed in Bordeaux no longer than it took to sell a few of the pebbles from El Dorado and to hire a good carriage for two passengers—because he couldn't travel without his philosopher Martin. His only regret was parting with his sheep, which he left to the Bordeaux Academy of Sciences. That year the Academy set as its prize essay topic, "to discover why this sheep's wool was red," and the prize was awarded to a learned man from the North, who demonstrated by A plus B minus C divided by Z that the sheep had to be red and die of rot.

Meanwhile, every traveler Candide met at the inns along the road told him, "We are going to Paris." This general eagerness eventually gave him a desire to see the capital too, and it wasn't much of a detour from the road to Venice.
He entered Paris through the suburb of Saint-Marceau, and thought he was in the filthiest village of Westphalia.

Candide had barely arrived at his inn when he found himself struck by a slight illness brought on by exhaustion. Since he had a very large diamond on his finger and the people of the inn had noticed a prodigiously heavy box among his luggage, two physicians came to attend him—though he had never called for them—along with two devout women who warmed his broths.
"I remember," Martin said, "that I was also sick in Paris during my first visit. I was very poor, so I had neither friends, nor devout women, nor doctors, and I recovered."

Nevertheless, between medicine and bloodletting, Candide's illness grew serious. A parish priest from the neighborhood came, with great meekness, to ask him for a bill-of-exchange drawn on the next world, payable to the bearer. Candide refused. The devout women assured him it was the new fashion; he replied that he was not a man of fashion. Martin wanted to throw the priest out the window. The priest swore they wouldn't let Candide be buried; Martin swore he would bury the priest if he kept making a nuisance of himself. The quarrel grew heated. Martin took him by the shoulders and roughly shoved him out the door—which caused a great scandal and a lawsuit.

Candide recovered, and during his convalescence he had very good company join him at supper. They played for high stakes. Candide was surprised that the ace never came to him; but Martin wasn't surprised at all.

Among those who did him the honors of the town was a little Abbé from Périgord—one of those busybodies who are always alert, officious, pushy, fawning, and obliging; who watch for strangers passing through the capital, tell them the scandalous gossip of the town, and offer them pleasures at every price. He first took Candide and Martin to the Comédie, where a new tragedy was being performed. Candide happened to be seated near some of the fashionable wits. This didn't prevent him from shedding tears at the well-acted scenes. One of the critics beside him said between acts:

"Your tears are misplaced. That actress is dreadful; the actor playing opposite her is worse; and the play is still worse than the actors. The author doesn't know a word of Arabic, yet the play is set in Arabia; and besides, he is a man who doesn't believe in innate ideas. Tomorrow I'll bring you twenty pamphlets written against him."
"How many plays do you have in France, sir?" asked Candide to the Abbé.
"Five or six thousand."
"What a number!" said Candide. "How many good ones?"
"Fifteen or sixteen," replied the other.
"What a number!" said Martin.
Candide was very taken with an actress who played Queen Elizabeth in a rather dull tragedy that was still sometimes staged.
"That actress," he said to Martin, "pleases me greatly; she has a resemblance to Miss Cunegonde. I would be very glad to pay my respects to her."
The Périgordian Abbé offered to introduce him. Candide, having been raised in Germany, asked what the etiquette was—how they treated queens of England in France.

"One has to make distinctions," said the Abbé. "In the provinces one takes them to the inn; in Paris, one treats them with respect when they are beautiful, and throws them onto the highway when they are dead."
"Queens on the highway!" said Candide.

"Yes, truly," said Martin, "the Abbé is right. I was in Paris when Miss Monime passed, as the saying goes, from this life to the next. She was refused what people call the honors of burial—that is, the right to rot with all the beggars of the neighborhood in an ugly cemetery. Her company buried her alone at the corner of the Rue de Bourgogne, which must have grieved her greatly, for she had a noble soul."
"That was most uncivil," said Candide.

"What do you expect?" said Martin. "These people are made that way. Imagine every contradiction, every possible incompatibility—you'll find them in the government, in the law courts, in the churches, and in the public spectacles of this droll nation."
"Is it true that people are always laughing in Paris?" asked Candide.
"Yes," said the Abbé, "but it means nothing, for they complain about everything with great bursts of laughter; they even do the most detestable things while laughing."
"Who," said Candide, "was that great pig who spoke so ill of the play that made me weep, and of the actors who gave me so much pleasure?"

"He is a bad character," answered the Abbé, "who earns his living by speaking ill of all plays and all books. He hates anything that succeeds, the way eunuchs hate those who enjoy themselves. He's one of those serpents of literature who feed on filth and spite—he's a folliculaire."
"What is a folliculaire?" asked Candide.
"It is," said the Abbé, "a hack pamphleteer—a Fréron."
So Candide, Martin, and the Périgordian conversed on the staircase, while watching everyone leave after the performance.
"Although I'm eager to see Cunegonde again," said Candide, "I would still like to sup with Miss Clairon, for she seems admirable to me."
The Abbé was not the man to get close to Miss Clairon, who received only the best company.
"She is engaged this evening," he said, "but I shall have the honor of taking you to the home of a lady of quality, and there you will get to know Paris as though you had lived in it for years."

Candide, who was naturally curious, let himself be taken to this lady's house at the end of the Faubourg Saint-Honoré. The company was busy playing faro. A dozen gloomy punters each held a little deck of cards—a dismal record of their misfortunes. Profound silence reigned. Pallor was on the faces of the punters, anxiety on the banker's, and the hostess, sitting beside the pitiless banker, watched with lynx eyes every doubled stake and every raised wager as each player dog-eared his cards. She made them flatten the corners again with severe but polite attention; she showed no irritation, for fear of losing her customers. The lady insisted on being called the Marquise de Parolignac. Her daughter, aged fifteen, was among the punters, signaling with a covert glance the cheating of the poor souls who tried to repair the cruelties of fate. The Périgordian Abbé, Candide, and Martin came in; no one rose, no one greeted them, no one even looked at them; all were deeply absorbed in their cards.
"The Baroness of Thunder-ten-Tronckh was more polite," said Candide.

However, the Abbé whispered to the Marquise, who half rose, honored Candide with a gracious smile, and Martin with a condescending nod. She gave Candide a seat and a hand of cards, and he lost fifty thousand francs in two deals. After that they had supper in high spirits, and everyone was astonished that Candide was unmoved by his loss. The servants said among themselves, in their servant's language:
"Some English lord must be here tonight."

The supper began like most Parisian suppers, in silence, followed by a noise of words that couldn't quite be made out, then by pleasantries most of which were insipid, by false news, by bad reasoning, a little politics, and a great deal of malicious gossip. They also discussed new books.
"Have you seen," said the Périgordian Abbé, "the novel by Monsieur Gauchat, doctor of divinity?"

"Yes," answered one of the guests, "but I couldn't finish it. We have a flood of silly writings, but none of them together comes near to the impertinence of Gauchat, Doctor of Divinity. I am so sick of the great number of detestable books pouring over us that I've been reduced to playing faro."
"And what do you say of Archdeacon Trublet's Mélanges?" asked the Abbé.

"Ah!" said the Marquise de Parolignac, "the tiresome creature! How curiously he repeats to you all that the world already knows! How ponderously he discusses what isn't worth even a light remark! How, with no wit of his own, he appropriates the wit of others! How he spoils what he steals! How he disgusts me! But he shan't disgust me any longer—a few pages of the Archdeacon are enough."

There was at the table a man of taste and learning who backed up the Marquise. They next spoke of tragedies. The lady asked why there are tragedies that are sometimes played but cannot be read. The man of taste explained very well how a piece can have some interest and yet have almost no merit. He proved in few words that it isn't enough to slip in one or two of those situations found in every romance, situations that always seduce the audience. One has to be new without being odd, often sublime and always natural, to know the human heart and make it speak—to be a great poet without letting any character in the play seem like a poet; to know the language perfectly, to speak it with purity, in continuous harmony, and without ever letting rhythm detract from sense.

"Whoever," he added, "does not observe all these rules may produce one or two tragedies applauded in the theater, but he will never be counted among the good writers. There are very few good tragedies. Some are idylls in dialogue, well written and well rhymed; others are political arguments that put you to sleep, or long-winded amplifications that repel you; others are demonic ravings in barbarous style, disjointed in sequence, with long apostrophes to the gods, because the author doesn't know how to speak to men, full of false maxims and bombastic clichés."

Candide listened attentively to this speech and formed a great idea of the speaker; and since the Marquise had been careful to seat him beside her, he leaned toward her and took the liberty of asking who the man was who spoke so well.

"He is a scholar," said the lady, "who doesn't play cards, whom the Abbé sometimes brings to supper. He is perfectly at home in tragedies and books, and he has written a tragedy that was hissed off the stage, and a book of which nothing has ever been seen outside his bookseller's shop except the copy he dedicated to me."
"The great man!" said Candide. "He's another Pangloss!"
Then, turning to him, he said:
"Sir, you no doubt think that everything is for the best in the moral and physical world, and that nothing could be other than it is?"

"I, sir!" replied the scholar. "I know nothing of all that. I find that everything goes wrong for me; that no one knows his proper rank, or his proper station, or what he does, or what he ought to do; and that apart from supper—which is always merry, and where people seem to get along well enough—all the rest of our time is spent in senseless quarrels: Jansenist against Molinist, Parliament against the Church, men of letters against men of letters, courtesans against courtesans, financiers against the people, wives against husbands, relatives against relatives—it is eternal war."

"I have seen worse," Candide replied. "But a wise man, who has since had the misfortune of being hanged, taught me that all is marvelously well, and that these are merely the shadows on a beautiful painting."
"Your hanged man was mocking the world," said Martin. "These shadows are horrible blots."
"It is men who make the blots," said Candide, "and they cannot be done without."
"Then it is not their fault," said Martin.
Most of the punters, who understood none of this kind of talk, went on drinking; Martin reasoned with the scholar, and Candide told some of his adventures to his hostess.
After supper the Marquise took Candide into her private room and made him sit beside her on a sofa.
"Well now," she said to him, "you are desperately in love with Miss Cunegonde of Thunder-ten-Tronckh?"
"Yes, madam," answered Candide.
The Marquise replied with a tender smile:
"You answer me like a young man from Westphalia. A Frenchman would have said, 'It's true that I loved Miss Cunegonde, but seeing you, madam, I think I no longer love her.'"
"Alas, madam," said Candide, "I will answer you however you wish."
"Your passion for her," said the Marquise, "began when you picked up her handkerchief. I want you to pick up my garter."
"With all my heart," said Candide. And he picked it up.
"But I want you to put it on for me," said the lady.
And Candide put it on.

"You see," she said, "you are a foreigner. I sometimes make my Parisian lovers languish a fortnight, but I give myself to you on the first night, because one must do the honors of one's country to a young man from Westphalia."
Having noticed two enormous diamonds on the young foreigner's hands, the lady praised them with such sincerity that they passed from Candide's fingers onto her own.

Returning home with the Périgordian Abbé, Candide felt some remorse at having been unfaithful to Miss Cunegonde. The Abbé sympathized with his distress; he had had only a small share of the fifty thousand francs lost at play and of the value of the two diamonds, half given and half extorted. His plan was to profit as much as he could from the advantages that his acquaintance with Candide might bring him. He spoke at length about Cunegonde, and Candide told him he would beg her forgiveness for his infidelity when he saw her in Venice.
The Abbé redoubled his politeness and attentions, and took a tender interest in all that Candide said, all that he did, and all that he meant to do.
"So, sir, you have a rendezvous in Venice?"
"Yes, Monsieur l'Abbé," answered Candide. "It is absolutely necessary that I go to meet Miss Cunegonde."
And then the pleasure of speaking about the one he loved led him, as usual, to recount part of his adventures with the fair Westphalian.
"I believe," said the Abbé, "that Miss Cunegonde has a great deal of wit, and that she writes charming letters?"

"I have never received any from her," said Candide. "For having been thrown out of the castle on her account, I had no chance to write to her. Soon afterward I heard she was dead; then I found her alive; then I lost her again; and finally I sent an express messenger to her, two thousand five hundred leagues from here, and I'm waiting for an answer."

The Abbé listened attentively, and seemed lost in deep thought. He soon took his leave of the two foreigners after a most tender embrace. The next day Candide received, on waking, a letter phrased in these terms:

"My dearest love, I have been ill in this town for the past eight days. I learn that you are here. I would fly into your arms if only I could move. I heard of your passing through Bordeaux, where I left the faithful Cacambo and the old woman, who are to follow me very soon. The Governor of Buenos Aires has taken everything, but what remains to me is your heart. Come! Your presence will either restore me to life or kill me with joy."

This charming, this unhoped-for letter filled Candide with inexpressible joy, while the illness of his dear Cunegonde plunged him into grief. Torn between these two passions, he took his gold and his diamonds and hurried with Martin to the hotel where Miss Cunegonde was lodged. He entered her room trembling, his heart pounding, his voice choked with sobs. He tried to open the curtains of the bed and called for a light.
"Be careful what you do," said the servant-girl. "The light hurts her," and she drew the curtain back immediately.
"My dear Cunegonde," said Candide, weeping, "how are you? If you cannot see me, at least speak to me."
"She cannot speak," said the maid.
The lady then held a plump hand out from the bed, and Candide bathed it with his tears, then filled it with diamonds, leaving a bag of gold on the armchair.
In the midst of these transports an officer came in, followed by the Abbé and a squad of soldiers.
"There," he said, "are the two suspected foreigners," and at the same moment he ordered them seized and taken to prison.
"Travelers are not treated this way in El Dorado," said Candide.
"I am more of a Manichean now than ever," said Martin.
"But please, sir, where are you taking us?" said Candide.
"To a dungeon," answered the officer.

Martin, having recovered himself a little, concluded that the lady who had played the part of Cunegonde was a swindler, that the Périgordian Abbé was a scoundrel who had taken advantage of Candide's honest simplicity, and that the officer was another scoundrel they could easily silence.

Candide, advised by Martin and impatient to see the real Cunegonde, rather than expose himself to a court of justice proposed to the officer that he give him three small diamonds, each worth about three thousand pistoles.

"Ah, sir," said the man with the ivory baton, "had you committed every crime imaginable, you would still be to me the most honest man in the world. Three diamonds! Each worth three thousand pistoles! Sir, instead of carrying you to jail I would lay down my life to serve you. There are orders to arrest all foreigners, but leave it to me. I have a brother in Dieppe, in Normandy! I'll escort you there, and if you have a diamond to give him, he'll take as much care of you as I would."
"And why," said Candide, "should all foreigners be arrested?"

"It is," the Périgordian Abbé then answered, "because a poor beggar from the country of Atrebatie heard some foolish things said. This led him to commit a parricide—not the kind of 1610 in the month of May, but the kind of 1594 in the month of December, and such as others committed in other years and other months by other poor devils who had heard nonsense spoken."
The officer then explained what the Abbé meant.

"Ah, the monsters!" cried Candide. "What horrors among a people who dance and sing! Is there no way to get quickly out of this country where monkeys goad tigers? I've seen no bears in my own country, but men—men I have beheld nowhere except in El Dorado. In the name of God, sir, take me to Venice, where I am to wait for Miss Cunegonde."
"I can take you no further than lower Normandy," said the officer.
He immediately had their irons struck off, acknowledged he had been mistaken, dismissed his men, and set out with Candide and Martin for Dieppe, where he left them in the care of his brother.

There was then a small Dutch ship in the harbor. The Norman, who by the virtue of three more diamonds had become the most obliging of men, put Candide and his attendants on board a vessel that was just about to set sail for Portsmouth in England.
This was not the way to Venice, but Candide believed he had escaped from hell, and counted on soon having an opportunity to resume his journey.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 — Candide and Martin Touched Upon the Coast of England, and What They Saw There
paragraphs: "Ah, Pangloss! Pangloss! Ah, Martin! Martin! Ah, my dear Cunegonde, what kind of world is this?" said Candide on board the Dutch ship.
"Something very foolish and abominable," said Martin.
"You know England? Are people as foolish there as in France?"

"It's a different kind of folly," said Martin. "You know that these two nations are at war over a few acres of snow in Canada, and that they are spending far more on this splendid war than the whole of Canada is worth. As for telling you exactly whether there are more people fit for a madhouse in one country or the other—that's beyond my limited intelligence. I only know, in general terms, that the people we are about to see are deeply bilious."

Talking like this, they arrived at Portsmouth. The coast was lined with crowds of people, their eyes fixed on a handsome man kneeling, blindfolded, on board one of the warships in the harbor. Four soldiers stood facing this man; each of them fired three balls into his head, with the calmest air in the world; and the entire crowd went away thoroughly satisfied.
"What is all this?" said Candide. "And what demon exerts his dominion in this country?"
He then asked who the handsome man was who had been killed with so much ceremony. They told him he was an Admiral.
"And why kill this Admiral?"
"Because he did not kill enough men himself. He gave battle to a French Admiral, and it has been proved that he was not close enough to him."
"But," replied Candide, "the French Admiral was just as far from the English Admiral."
"No doubt of it; but in this country it is considered good, from time to time, to kill an Admiral in order to encourage the others."

Candide was so shocked and bewildered by what he saw and heard that he refused to set foot on shore, and he struck a bargain with the Dutch skipper—even if the man were to rob him the way the Surinam captain had—to take him to Venice without delay.

The skipper was ready in two days. They skirted the coast of France; they passed within sight of Lisbon, and Candide trembled. They passed through the Straits and entered the Mediterranean. At last they landed at Venice.

"God be praised!" said Candide, embracing Martin. "Here is where I shall see my beautiful Cunegonde again. I trust Cacambo as I trust myself. All is well, all will be well, all goes as well as possible."

chapters.title: Chapter 24 — Of Paquette and Friar Giroflee
paragraphs: On arriving in Venice, Candide searched for Cacambo in every inn and coffeehouse, and among every lady of pleasure, but without success. He sent inquiries every day to every ship that came in. Still no news of Cacambo.

"What!" he said to Martin. "I have had time to sail from Surinam to Bordeaux, to go from Bordeaux to Paris, from Paris to Dieppe, from Dieppe to Portsmouth, to skirt Portugal and Spain, to cross the whole Mediterranean, to spend some months here—and still the beautiful Cunegonde has not arrived! Instead of her, I have met only a Parisian wench and a Périgordian Abbé. Cunegonde is dead, there's no doubt of it, and all that's left for me is to die. Alas! How much better it would have been to stay in the paradise of El Dorado than to come back to this accursed Europe! You are right, my dear Martin: all is misery and illusion."
He fell into a deep melancholy, and went neither to the opera nor to any of the other Carnival amusements; in fact, he was proof against the temptations of any of the ladies.

"You are truly very simple," said Martin, "if you imagine that a half-breed valet with five or six millions in his pocket is going to travel to the other end of the world to find your mistress and bring her back to you in Venice. If he finds her, he'll keep her for himself; if he doesn't, he'll take another. I advise you to forget your valet Cacambo and your mistress Cunegonde."

Martin was not consoling. Candide's melancholy grew worse; and Martin kept proving to him that there is very little virtue or happiness on earth, except perhaps in El Dorado, which no one can get into.

While they were arguing on this important subject and waiting for Cunegonde, Candide noticed a young Theatine friar in St. Mark's Square with a girl on his arm. The Theatine looked fresh-faced, plump, and vigorous; his eyes were sparkling, his air confident, his look lofty, and his step bold. The girl was very pretty and was singing; she gazed amorously at her Theatine and now and then pinched his plump cheeks.

"You'll at least grant me," said Candide to Martin, "that these two are happy. Up to now I've met nothing but miserable people all over the habitable globe, except in El Dorado; but as for this pair, I'd lay a wager that they are very happy."
"I bet you they aren't," said Martin.
"We have only to invite them to dinner," said Candide, "and you'll see whether I'm mistaken."

He went up to them at once, paid his compliments, and invited them to his inn for some macaroni, Lombard partridges, and caviar, with wines from Montepulciano, Lacrima Christi, Cyprus, and Samos. The girl blushed, the Theatine accepted, and she followed him, glancing at Candide with confusion and surprise, and shedding a few tears. No sooner had she set foot in Candide's apartment than she cried out:
"Ah! Mr. Candide doesn't recognize Paquette any more."
Candide hadn't yet looked at her carefully, his thoughts being entirely absorbed with Cunegonde; but he remembered her as she spoke.
"Alas!" he said, "my poor child, was it you who reduced Doctor Pangloss to the beautiful state in which I saw him?"

"Alas! Sir, it was indeed me," answered Paquette. "I see you have heard everything. I was told of the appalling disasters that befell my lady the Baroness's family, and the fair Cunegonde. I swear to you that my own fate has hardly been less sad. I was very innocent when you knew me. A Grey Friar, my confessor, seduced me without difficulty. The consequences were terrible. I was forced to leave the castle soon after the Baron had sent you off with kicks to the backside. If a famous surgeon hadn't taken pity on me, I would have died. For some time I was his mistress, purely out of gratitude. His wife, half mad with jealousy, beat me every day without mercy; she was a fury. The surgeon was one of the ugliest of men, and I the most wretched of women, to be beaten daily for a man I didn't love. You know, sir, what a dangerous thing it is for a bad-tempered woman to be married to a doctor. Incensed by his wife's behavior, he one day gave her so effective a remedy for a slight cold that she died two hours later in the most horrid convulsions. The wife's relatives prosecuted the husband; he fled, and I was thrown into prison. My innocence would not have saved me if I hadn't been pretty. The judge set me free on the condition that he succeed the surgeon. Soon I was supplanted by a rival, thrown out of doors penniless, and forced to continue this abominable trade, which seems so pleasant to you men, and which for us women is the very depth of misery. I came to ply the profession in Venice. Ah, sir, if you could only imagine what it is to be obliged to caress, without distinction, an old merchant, a lawyer, a monk, a gondolier, an abbé; to be exposed to abuse and insults; often to be reduced to borrowing a petticoat just to have it lifted by some disagreeable man; to be robbed by one of what you've earned from another; to be subject to the extortions of the officers of justice; and to have only a frightful old age, a hospital, and a dung heap in your future—you would conclude that I am one of the most unhappy creatures in the world."
Paquette thus opened her heart to honest Candide, in the presence of Martin, who said to his friend:
"You see, I've already won half the wager."
Friar Giroflée stayed in the dining room and drank a glass or two of wine while waiting for dinner.

"But," said Candide to Paquette, "you looked so cheerful and content when I saw you; you were singing, and you behaved so affectionately to the Theatine, that you seemed to me as happy as you now claim to be the opposite."
"Ah, sir," answered Paquette, "that's one of the miseries of the trade. Yesterday an officer robbed and beat me; today I must put on good humor to please a friar."

Candide needed no more convincing; he admitted that Martin was right. They sat down at the table with Paquette and the Theatine; the meal was entertaining, and toward the end they were conversing with complete openness.

"Father," said Candide to the friar, "you seem to me to enjoy a state that all the world might envy. The flower of health shines in your face; your expression makes your happiness plain; you have a very pretty girl for your recreation, and you seem well content with your state as a Theatine."

"By my faith, sir," said Friar Giroflée, "I wish all the Theatines were at the bottom of the sea. A hundred times I've been tempted to set the convent on fire and go off to become a Turk. My parents forced me, at the age of fifteen, to put on this detestable habit in order to increase the fortune of a cursed elder brother—may God confound him. Jealousy, discord, and fury live in the convent. It's true I've preached a few bad sermons that have brought me a little money, half of which the prior steals, while the rest serves to keep my girls; but when I come back at night to the monastery, I'm ready to dash my head against the walls of the dormitory, and all my fellow friars are in the same case."
Martin turned to Candide with his usual coolness.
"Well," he said, "haven't I won the whole wager?"
Candide gave two thousand piastres to Paquette and a thousand to Friar Giroflée.
"I'll answer for it," he said, "that with this they will be happy."
"I don't believe it at all," said Martin. "With these piastres you will perhaps only make them the more unhappy."

"Let that be as it may," said Candide. "One thing consoles me: I see that we often meet people we thought we'd never see again; so perhaps, just as I've found my red sheep and Paquette, I may also find Cunegonde."
"I hope," said Martin, "that she will one day make you very happy; but I very much doubt it."
"You are very hard of belief," said Candide.
"I have lived," said Martin.
"You see those gondoliers," said Candide. "Aren't they always singing?"

"You don't see them," said Martin, "at home with their wives and brats. The Doge has his troubles, the gondoliers have theirs. It's true that, all things considered, a gondolier's life is preferable to a Doge's; but I believe the difference is so slight it's not worth examining."

"People talk," said Candide, "about Senator Pococurante, who lives in that fine palace on the Brenta, where he entertains foreigners with great courtesy. They claim that this man has never felt any uneasiness."
"I'd be glad to see such a rarity," said Martin.
Candide immediately sent word to Lord Pococurante asking permission to wait upon him the next day.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 — The Visit to Lord Pococurante, a Noble Venetian
paragraphs: Candide and Martin went by gondola along the Brenta and arrived at the palace of the noble Signor Pococurante. The gardens, laid out with taste, were adorned with fine marble statues. The palace was beautifully built. The master of the house was a man of sixty, and very wealthy. He received the two travelers with polite indifference, which unsettled Candide a little but was not at all disagreeable to Martin.
First, two pretty girls, very neatly dressed, served them chocolate that had been frothed exceedingly well. Candide couldn't help praising their beauty, grace, and poise.

"They are good enough creatures," said the Senator. "I have them lie with me sometimes, because I am utterly tired of the ladies of the town, of their coquetries, their jealousies, their quarrels, their moods, their pettinesses, their pride, their follies, and of the sonnets one has to write, or have written, for them. But even so, these two girls are beginning to weary me."
After refreshments, Candide wandered into a long gallery and was struck by the beautiful paintings. He asked who had painted the first two.

"They are by Raphael," said the Senator. "I bought them some years ago at a great price, out of vanity. They are said to be the finest things in Italy, but they don't please me at all. The colors are too dark, the figures are not sufficiently rounded or in good relief, the draperies look nothing like real cloth. In a word, whatever one may say, I do not find a true imitation of nature in them. I only love a painting when I think I see nature itself—and there are none of that kind. I have a great many paintings, but I value them very little."
While they were waiting for dinner, Pococurante ordered a concert. Candide found the music delicious.

"This noise," said the Senator, "can amuse one for half an hour; but if it went on any longer it would become tiresome to everybody, though no one would dare admit it. Music today is merely the art of executing difficult things, and what is only difficult cannot please for long. Perhaps I would be fonder of opera if they hadn't found the secret of turning it into a monster that revolts me. Let anyone who wishes go and see bad tragedies set to music, where the scenes are contrived for no purpose other than to introduce two or three songs ridiculously out of place, just to show off an actress's voice. Let anyone who wants to, or can, swoon with pleasure at the sight of a eunuch warbling the role of Caesar or Cato and strutting awkwardly on the stage. For my part, I have long since renounced those paltry entertainments that are the glory of modern Italy, and that sovereigns pay so dearly for."
Candide disputed the point a little, but cautiously. Martin entirely shared the Senator's opinion.
They sat down at the table, and after an excellent dinner they went into the library. Candide, seeing a magnificently bound Homer, complimented the virtuoso on his good taste.
"There," he said, "is a book that was once the delight of the great Pangloss, the best philosopher in Germany."

"It is not mine," answered Pococurante coolly. "They used to try to make me believe I took pleasure in reading him. But that constant repetition of battles, all so strikingly alike; those gods who are always busy but never do anything decisive; that Helen, who is the cause of the war but hardly appears in the piece; that Troy, besieged so long without ever being taken—all of it together bored me greatly. I've sometimes asked learned men whether they were not just as weary of the work as I am. The honest ones have admitted to me that the poem put them to sleep—but they still felt they had to have it in their library, as a monument of antiquity, or like those rusty old coins that no longer circulate."
"But your Excellency does not think the same of Virgil?" said Candide.

"I grant," said the Senator, "that the second, fourth, and sixth books of his Aeneid are excellent; but as for his pious Aeneas, his strong Cloanthus, his friend Achates, his little Ascanius, his silly King Latinus, his bourgeois Amata, his insipid Lavinia—I cannot imagine anything flatter or more disagreeable. I much prefer Tasso, or even the soporific tales of Ariosto."
"May I be so bold, sir," said Candide, "as to ask whether you do not get great pleasure from reading Horace?"

"There are maxims in this writer," answered Pococurante, "from which a man of the world can derive great benefit, and because they are written in vigorous verse they stick more easily in the memory. But I care little for his journey to Brundisium, or for his account of a bad dinner, or for his vulgar quarrel between one Rupilius, whose words he says were full of poisonous filth, and another whose language was steeped in vinegar. I've read with great distaste his coarse verses against old women and witches; and I can see no merit in his telling his friend Maecenas that if only he will rank him among the lyric poets, his lofty head will touch the stars. Fools admire everything in an author of reputation. For my part, I read only to please myself. I like only what serves my purpose."
Candide, having been raised never to judge for himself, was astonished by what he was hearing. Martin found a good deal of reason in Pococurante's remarks.
"Oh! here is Cicero," said Candide. "There's the great man whom I imagine you never tire of reading."

"I never read him," replied the Venetian. "What is it to me whether he pleads for Rabirius or Cluentius? I try causes enough myself. His philosophical works seem better to me, but when I noticed that he doubted everything, I concluded I knew as much as he did, and that I needed no guide to learn ignorance."
"Ha! here are eighty volumes of the Academy of Sciences," cried Martin. "Perhaps there is something valuable in this collection."
"There might be," said Pococurante, "if even one of those rubbish-rakers had shown how to make pins. In all these volumes there are nothing but fanciful systems, and not a single useful thing."
"And what a lot of dramatic works I see here," said Candide, "in Italian, Spanish, and French."

"Yes," replied the Senator, "there are three thousand, and not three dozen of them any good. As for those collections of sermons, which all together aren't worth a single page of Seneca, and those huge volumes of theology, you can well imagine that neither I nor anyone else ever opens them."
Martin noticed some shelves filled with English books.
"I have an idea," he said, "that a Republican must be greatly pleased with most of these books, which are written in a spirit of freedom."

"Yes," answered Pococurante, "it is a noble thing to write as one thinks; this is the privilege of being human. In all of our Italy, we write only what we do not think. Those who live in the land of the Caesars and the Antonines dare not acquire a single idea without the permission of a Dominican friar. I would be pleased with the liberty that inspires the English genius, if passion and party spirit did not corrupt everything valuable in that precious liberty."
Candide, noticing a Milton, asked whether he didn't regard this author as a great man.

"Who?" said Pococurante, "that barbarian who writes a long commentary in ten books of harsh verse on the first chapter of Genesis? That coarse imitator of the Greeks, who disfigures the Creation, and who—while Moses represents the Eternal producing the world by a word—makes the Messiah take a great pair of compasses from the armory of heaven to draw the outline of his work? How can I have any esteem for a writer who has ruined Tasso's hell and devil, who turns Lucifer sometimes into a toad and sometimes into a pigmy, who makes him repeat the same things a hundred times, who makes him argue theology, who, by a solemn imitation of Ariosto's comic invention of firearms, has the devils cannonading in heaven? Neither I nor any man in Italy could take pleasure in these melancholy extravagances; and the marriage of Sin and Death, and the snakes brought forth by Sin, are enough to turn the stomach of anyone with the least taste, and his long description of a pest-house is fit only for a gravedigger. This obscure, whimsical, and disagreeable poem was despised when it was first published, and I only treat it now the way it was treated in its own country by its contemporaries. For that matter, I say what I think, and I care very little whether others agree with me."
Candide was distressed by this speech, for he had respect for Homer and was fond of Milton.
"Alas!" he said quietly to Martin, "I'm afraid this man holds our German poets in very great contempt."
"There wouldn't be much harm in that," said Martin.
"Oh! what a superior man," said Candide under his breath. "What a great genius this Pococurante is! Nothing can please him."
After their survey of the library they went down into the garden, where Candide praised its many beauties.
"I know of nothing in such poor taste," said the master. "Everything you see here is merely trifling. After tomorrow I will have it planted on a nobler design."
"Well," said Candide to Martin when they had taken their leave, "you must admit this is the happiest of mortals, for he is above everything he possesses."
"But don't you see," answered Martin, "that he is disgusted with all he possesses? Plato observed long ago that those stomachs are not the best which reject all sorts of food."
"But isn't there pleasure," said Candide, "in criticizing everything, in spotting faults where others see only beauties?"
"That is to say," replied Martin, "that there is some pleasure in having no pleasure."
"Well, well," said Candide, "I find that I shall be the only happy man, once I am blessed with the sight of my dear Cunegonde."
"It is always good to hope," said Martin.
Meanwhile, the days and weeks passed. Cacambo did not come, and Candide was so overwhelmed with grief that he didn't even notice that Paquette and Friar Giroflée had not returned to thank him.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 — Of a Supper Which Candide and Martin Took with Six Strangers, and Who They Were
paragraphs: One evening, just as Candide and Martin were sitting down to supper with some foreigners who were lodging at the same inn, a man whose complexion was as black as soot came up behind Candide and, taking him by the arm, said:
"Get yourself ready to leave with us. Don't fail."
At that, Candide turned around and saw—Cacambo! Only the sight of Cunegonde could have astonished and delighted him more. He was on the verge of going mad with joy. He embraced his dear friend.
"Cunegonde is here, surely! Where is she? Take me to her that I may die of joy in her company."
"Cunegonde is not here," said Cacambo. "She is in Constantinople."
"Oh heavens! In Constantinople! But even if she were in China I would fly there. Let's be off."
"We shall set out after supper," replied Cacambo. "I can tell you nothing more. I am a slave; my master is waiting for me; I must wait on him at table. Don't say a word, eat, and then get ready."

Candide, torn between joy and grief, delighted at seeing his faithful agent again, astonished at finding him a slave, filled with fresh hope of recovering his mistress, his heart pounding, his mind in a whirl, sat down at the table with Martin—who watched all these scenes perfectly unconcerned—and with six foreigners who had come to Venice for Carnival.
Cacambo waited at table on one of the foreigners; toward the end of the meal he drew near his master and whispered in his ear:
"Sire, Your Majesty may leave whenever you please. The vessel is ready."
With these words he went out. The company, in great surprise, looked at one another without saying a word, when another servant approached his master and said:
"Sire, Your Majesty's carriage is at Padua, and the boat is ready."
The master gave a nod, and the servant went away. The whole company stared at one another again, and their surprise doubled. A third valet came up to a third foreigner, saying:
"Sire, believe me, Your Majesty should not stay here any longer. I am going to get everything ready."
And he immediately disappeared. Candide and Martin had no doubt that this was some Carnival masquerade. Then a fourth servant said to a fourth master:
"Your Majesty may leave whenever you please."

With that he went away like the rest. The fifth valet said the same thing to the fifth master. But the sixth valet spoke differently to the sixth foreigner, who was seated next to Candide. He said to him:
"Faith, Sire, they will give credit no longer, neither to Your Majesty nor to me, and we may perhaps both of us be thrown in jail this very night. So I'll look out for myself. Farewell."
All the servants having now left, the six foreigners, along with Candide and Martin, remained in profound silence. At length Candide broke it.
"Gentlemen," he said, "this is a very good joke indeed, but why should you all be kings? For my part, I confess that neither Martin nor I is a king."
Cacambo's master then answered gravely, in Italian:

"I am not joking at all. My name is Achmet III. I was Grand Sultan for many years. I dethroned my brother; my nephew dethroned me; my viziers were beheaded, and I am condemned to end my days in the old Seraglio. My nephew, the great Sultan Mahmoud, permits me to travel sometimes for my health, and I have come to spend the Carnival at Venice."
A young man who sat next to Achmet then spoke as follows:

"My name is Ivan. I was once Emperor of all the Russias, but I was dethroned in my cradle. My parents were shut up in prison, and I was raised there; yet I am sometimes allowed to travel in the company of persons who act as guards, and I have come to spend Carnival at Venice."
The third said:

"I am Charles Edward, King of England. My father has resigned all his legal rights to me. I have fought to defend them, and more than eight hundred of my followers have been hanged, drawn, and quartered. I have been locked in prison. I am on my way to Rome to visit the King my father, who was dethroned, as was I, as was my grandfather; and I have come to spend Carnival at Venice."
The fourth then spoke in his turn:

"I am the King of Poland. The fortune of war has stripped me of my hereditary dominions. My father went through the same reverses. I resign myself to Providence in the same manner as Sultan Achmet, the Emperor Ivan, and King Charles Edward, whom may God long preserve; and I have come to Carnival at Venice."
The fifth said:

"I too am King of Poland. I have been dethroned twice; but Providence has given me another country, where I have done more good than all the Sarmatian kings put together could ever do on the banks of the Vistula. I likewise resign myself to Providence, and have come to spend Carnival at Venice."
It was now the sixth monarch's turn to speak:

"Gentlemen," he said, "I am not so great a prince as any of you; but still, I am a king. I am Theodore, elected King of Corsica. I had the title of Majesty, and now I am hardly treated as a gentleman. I have minted coins, and now I am not worth a farthing. I have had two secretaries of state, and now I scarcely have a valet. I have seen myself on a throne, and I have seen myself on straw in a common jail in London. I'm afraid I shall meet the same treatment here, though like Your Majesties, I have come to see Carnival at Venice."

The other five kings listened to this speech with generous compassion. Each of them gave twenty sequins to King Theodore to buy him clothes and linen; and Candide made him a present of a diamond worth two thousand sequins.
"Who can this commoner be," the five kings said to one another, "who is able to give, and really has given, a hundred times as much as any of us?"

Just as they were rising from the table, in came four Serene Highnesses, who had also been stripped of their territories by the fortune of war, and had come to spend Carnival at Venice. But Candide paid no attention to these newcomers; his thoughts were entirely taken up with his voyage to Constantinople, in search of his beloved Cunegonde.

chapters.title: Chapter 27 — Candide's Voyage to Constantinople
paragraphs: The faithful Cacambo had already persuaded the Turkish skipper, who was to take Sultan Achmet back to Constantinople, to let Candide and Martin come aboard his ship. They both embarked after paying their respects to his miserable Highness.

"You see," said Candide to Martin on the way, "we had supper with six dethroned kings, and of those six there was one I gave charity to. There may be many other princes even more unfortunate. For my part, I've only lost a hundred sheep; and now I am flying into Cunegonde's arms. My dear Martin, once again Pangloss was right: all is for the best."
"I hope so," answered Martin.
"But," said Candide, "it was a very strange adventure we had in Venice. It has never been seen or heard of before—that six dethroned kings should have supper together at a common inn."

"It's no more extraordinary," said Martin, "than most of the things that have happened to us. It is a very common thing for kings to be dethroned; and as for the honor we had of dining in their company, it's a trifle not worth our attention."
No sooner had Candide come aboard the ship than he ran to his old valet and friend Cacambo and embraced him tenderly.
"Well," he said, "what news of Cunegonde? Is she still a prodigy of beauty? Does she still love me? How is she? You have surely bought her a palace at Constantinople?"

"My dear master," answered Cacambo, "Cunegonde washes dishes on the banks of the Propontis, in the service of a prince who has very few dishes to wash. She is a slave in the household of a former sovereign named Ragotski, whom the Grand Turk allows three crowns a day in his exile. But what is worse still, she has lost her beauty and become horribly ugly."

"Well, beautiful or ugly," replied Candide, "I am a man of honor, and it is my duty to love her still. But how did she come to be reduced to such an abject state, with the five or six millions you took her?"

"Ah!" said Cacambo, "didn't I have to give two millions to Señor Don Fernando d'Ibaraa y Figueora y Mascarenes y Lampourdos y Souza, Governor of Buenos Aires, for permission to take Miss Cunegonde away? And didn't a corsair boldly rob us of all the rest? Didn't this corsair carry us to Cape Matapan, to Milos, to Nicaria, to Samos, to Petra, to the Dardanelles, to Marmora, to Scutari? Cunegonde and the old woman serve the prince I just mentioned, and I am a slave to the dethroned Sultan."
"What a string of shocking calamities!" cried Candide. "But after all, I still have some diamonds left, and I can easily pay Cunegonde's ransom. Still, it is a pity she has grown so ugly."
