Then, turning to Martin, "Who do you think," he said, "is most to be pitied—Sultan Achmet, the Emperor Ivan, King Charles Edward, or I?"
"How should I know!" answered Martin. "I would have to see into your hearts to be able to tell."
"Ah!" said Candide, "if Pangloss were here, he could tell us."

"I don't know," said Martin, "in what kind of scales your Pangloss would weigh the misfortunes of mankind and place a just estimate on their sorrows. All I can venture to say is that there are millions of people on this earth who have a hundred times more to complain of than King Charles Edward, the Emperor Ivan, or Sultan Achmet."
"That may well be," said Candide.

In a few days they reached the Bosphorus, and Candide began by paying a very high ransom for Cacambo. Then, without losing any time, he and his companions boarded a galley in order to search along the banks of the Propontis for his Cunegonde, however ugly she might have become.

Among the crew were two slaves who rowed very badly, to whose bare shoulders the Levantine captain now and then applied blows from a bull's pizzle. By a natural impulse, Candide looked at these two slaves more attentively than at the other oarsmen, and drew closer to them in pity. Their features, though greatly disfigured, bore a slight resemblance to those of Pangloss and of the unhappy Jesuit and Westphalian Baron, Miss Cunegonde's brother. This moved and saddened him. He looked at them still more attentively.
"Truly," he said to Cacambo, "if I had not seen Master Pangloss hanged, and if I had not had the misfortune of killing the Baron, I would think that those were the two rowing."
At the names of the Baron and Pangloss, the two galley slaves let out a loud cry, clung to their bench, and let their oars drop. The captain ran up and redoubled his blows with the bull's pizzle.
"Stop! Stop, sir!" cried Candide. "I will give you whatever money you please."
"What! Is it Candide?" said one of the slaves.
"What! Is it Candide?" said the other.
"Am I dreaming?" cried Candide. "Am I awake? Am I on board a galley? Is this the Baron whom I killed? Is this Master Pangloss whom I saw hanged?"
"It is us! It is us!" they answered.
"What! Is this the great philosopher?" said Martin.

"Ah, Captain," said Candide, "what ransom will you take for Monsieur de Thunder-ten-Tronckh, one of the first barons of the empire, and for Monsieur Pangloss, the most profound metaphysician in Germany?"

"Dog of a Christian," answered the Levantine captain, "since these two dogs of Christian slaves are barons and metaphysicians—which I don't doubt are high dignities in their country—you shall give me fifty thousand sequins."
"You shall have them, sir. Take me back to Constantinople at once, and you shall have the money immediately. But no—take me first to Miss Cunegonde."
Yet at Candide's first offer, the Levantine captain had already come about and set the crew to plying their oars faster than a bird cleaves the air.
Candide embraced the Baron and Pangloss a hundred times.
"And how is it, my dear Baron, that I did not kill you? And, my dear Pangloss, how did you come back to life after being hanged? And why are you both aboard a Turkish galley?"
"And is it really true that my dear sister is in this country?" said the Baron.
"Yes," answered Cacambo.
"Then I behold once more my dear Candide!" cried Pangloss.

Candide introduced Martin and Cacambo to them; they embraced one another, and all spoke at once. The galley flew along; they were already in port. Candide at once sent for a Jew, to whom he sold for fifty thousand sequins a diamond worth a hundred thousand, though the fellow swore to him by Abraham that he could give him no more. He immediately paid the ransom for the Baron and Pangloss. The latter threw himself at the feet of his deliverer and bathed them with his tears; the former thanked him with a nod and promised to repay the money at the first opportunity.
"But is it really possible that my sister can be in Turkey?" he said.
"Nothing is more possible," said Cacambo, "seeing that she scours dishes in the service of a Transylvanian prince."
Candide at once sent for two more Jews and sold them some more diamonds, and then they all set out together in another galley to deliver Cunegonde from slavery.

chapters.title: Chapter 28 — What Happened to Candide, Cunegonde, Pangloss, Martin, Etc
paragraphs: "I ask your pardon once again," said Candide to the Baron, "your pardon, reverend Father, for having run you through the body."

"Say no more about it," answered the Baron. "I was a little too hasty, I admit; but since you wish to know by what fatality I came to be a galley slave, I will tell you. After I had been cured by the surgeon of the college of the wound you gave me, I was attacked and carried off by a party of Spanish troops, who shut me up in prison at Buenos Aires at the very time my sister was leaving there. I asked leave to return to Rome to the General of my order. I was appointed chaplain to the French Ambassador at Constantinople. I had not been in this position eight days when one evening I met a young Ichoglan, a very handsome fellow. The weather was warm. The young man wanted to bathe, and I took the opportunity to bathe as well. I didn't know that it was a capital crime for a Christian to be found naked with a young Muslim. A cadi sentenced me to a hundred blows on the soles of the feet, and condemned me to the galleys. I don't think there was ever a greater act of injustice. But I'd be very glad to know how my sister came to be a scullery maid to a Transylvanian prince who has taken refuge among the Turks."
"But you, my dear Pangloss," said Candide, "how can it be that I am seeing you again?"

"It is true," said Pangloss, "that you saw me hanged. I was supposed to be burned, but you may remember that it rained extremely hard when they were going to roast me. The storm was so violent they gave up trying to light the fire, so I was hanged, because they could do no better. A surgeon bought my body, took me home, and dissected me. He began by making a crucial incision on me from the navel to the collarbone. No one could have been more badly hanged than I was. The executioner of the Holy Inquisition was a sub-deacon who knew marvelously well how to burn people, but was not used to hanging them. The rope was wet and didn't slide properly, and besides it was poorly tied. In short, I was still breathing when the crucial incision made me give out such a frightful scream that my surgeon fell flat on his back, and imagining he had been dissecting the devil, he ran off, dying of fright, and tumbled down the stairs in his panic. His wife, hearing the noise, rushed in from the next room. She saw me stretched on the table with my crucial incision. She was seized with even greater fear than her husband, fled, and fell on top of him. When they had come to themselves a little, I heard the wife say to her husband: 'My dear, whatever possessed you to dissect a heretic? Don't you know these people always have the devil in them? I'll go and fetch a priest this minute to exorcise him.' At this I shuddered, and mustering what little courage I had left, I cried out loud: 'Have mercy on me!' At last the Portuguese barber took heart. He stitched up my wounds; his wife even nursed me. I was back on my feet at the end of a fortnight. The barber got me a place as a lackey to a knight of Malta who was going to Venice; but when I found that my master had no money to pay my wages, I entered the service of a Venetian merchant and went with him to Constantinople. One day I took it into my head to step into a mosque, where I saw an old imam and a very pretty young devotee saying her paternosters. Her bosom was uncovered, and between her breasts she had a beautiful bouquet of tulips, roses, anemones, ranunculi, hyacinths, and auriculas. She dropped her bouquet. I picked it up and presented it to her with a profound bow. I took so long giving it back that the imam began to grow angry, and seeing I was a Christian, he called out for help. They hauled me before the cadi, who ordered me a hundred lashes on the soles of my feet and sent me to the galleys. I was chained to the very same galley and the same bench as the young Baron. On board this galley there were four young men from Marseille, five Neapolitan priests, and two monks from Corfu, who told us that similar adventures happened every day. The Baron maintained that he had suffered greater injustice than I had, and I insisted that it was far more innocent to pick up a bouquet and place it back on a woman's bosom than to be caught stark naked with an Ichoglan. We were constantly arguing, and got twenty lashes with a bull's pizzle, when the concatenation of universal events brought you to our galley and you were kind enough to ransom us."
"Well, my dear Pangloss," Candide said to him, "when you had been hanged, dissected, whipped, and were pulling at the oar, did you still think everything in the world was for the best?"

"I am still of my first opinion," answered Pangloss, "for I am a philosopher and I cannot retract my views, especially since Leibniz could never be wrong; and besides, the pre-established harmony is the finest thing in the world, and so is his plenum and his materia subtilis."

chapters.title: Chapter 29 — How Candide Found Cunegonde and the Old Woman Again
paragraphs: While Candide, the Baron, Pangloss, Martin, and Cacambo were recounting their various adventures, reasoning about the contingent or non-contingent events of the universe, arguing about effects and causes, moral and physical evil, liberty and necessity, and the consolations a slave might feel even on a Turkish galley, they arrived at the house of the Transylvanian prince on the banks of the Propontis. The first sight that met their eyes was Cunegonde and the old woman hanging towels out to dry.

The Baron went pale at this sight. Tender, loving Candide, seeing his beautiful Cunegonde weather-beaten, her eyes bloodshot, her neck withered, her cheeks wrinkled, and her arms rough and red, recoiled three paces in horror, and then came forward out of good manners. She embraced Candide and her brother; they embraced the old woman; and Candide paid the ransom for them both.

There was a small farm in the neighborhood which the old woman suggested Candide should make do with until the company could be provided for in a better way. Cunegonde didn't know she had grown ugly, for no one had told her so, and she reminded Candide of his promise in such a positive tone that the good man didn't dare refuse her. He therefore informed the Baron that he intended to marry his sister.

"I will not suffer," said the Baron, "such a base act on her part, and such insolence on yours. I will never be reproached with this scandalous thing; my sister's children would never be able to enter the chapters of the nobility in Germany. No; my sister shall marry only a baron of the empire."
Cunegonde threw herself at his feet and bathed them with her tears; still he was inflexible.

"You foolish fellow," said Candide. "I have freed you from the galleys, I have paid your ransom, and your sister's as well. She was a scullery maid, and she is very ugly, yet I am so generous as to marry her—and you dare to oppose the match? I would kill you all over again, if I consulted only my anger."
"You may kill me again," said the Baron, "but you shall not marry my sister, at least while I am living."

chapters.title: Chapter 30 — The Conclusion
paragraphs: At the bottom of his heart, Candide had no wish to marry Cunegonde. But the Baron's extreme impertinence made him determined to go through with the match, and Cunegonde pressed him so strongly that he couldn't go back on his word. He consulted Pangloss, Martin, and the faithful Cacambo. Pangloss drew up an excellent memorial, in which he proved that the Baron had no rights over his sister and that, according to all the laws of the empire, she could marry Candide with her left hand. Martin was for throwing the Baron into the sea; Cacambo decided that it would be better to hand him back to the captain of the galley, after which they planned to send him back to the General Father of the order at Rome on the first ship. This advice was well received; the old woman approved it; they said not a word to his sister; the thing was carried out for a little money, and they had the double pleasure of entrapping a Jesuit and punishing the pride of a German baron.

It would be natural to imagine that after so many disasters, Candide, now married and living with the philosopher Pangloss, the philosopher Martin, the prudent Cacambo, and the old woman, and having brought so many diamonds from the country of the ancient Incas, must have led a very happy life. But the Jews cheated him so thoroughly that he had nothing left but his little farm. His wife grew uglier every day, and more peevish and unbearable. The old woman was infirm, and even more fretful than Cunegonde. Cacambo, who worked in the garden and carried vegetables to sell in Constantinople, was exhausted by the hard work and cursed his destiny. Pangloss was in despair at not shining in some German university. As for Martin, he was firmly convinced that he would be just as badly off anywhere else, and so bore things patiently. Candide, Martin, and Pangloss sometimes argued about morals and metaphysics. They often saw passing under the windows of their farm boats full of Effendis, Pashas, and Cadis being sent into banishment at Lemnos, Mytilene, or Erzurum. And they saw other Cadis, Pashas, and Effendis coming to take the place of the exiles, and being exiled in their turn. They saw heads neatly impaled to be presented to the Sublime Porte. Such spectacles swelled the number of their dissertations, and when they weren't arguing, time hung so heavily on their hands that one day the old woman ventured to say:

"I want to know which is worse: to be ravished a hundred times by negro pirates, to have a buttock cut off, to run the gauntlet among the Bulgarians, to be whipped and hanged at an auto-da-fé, to be dissected, to row in the galleys—in short, to go through all the miseries we have undergone—or to stay here with nothing to do?"
"That is a great question," said Candide.

This speech gave rise to new reflections, and Martin in particular concluded that man was born to live either in a state of distracting agitation or of lethargic disgust. Candide did not quite agree with that, but he affirmed nothing. Pangloss admitted that he had always suffered horribly; but having once maintained that everything was going wonderfully well, he maintained it still, though he no longer believed it.

What helped confirm Martin in his detestable principles, to shake Candide more than ever, and to puzzle Pangloss, was that one day they saw Paquette and Friar Giroflée arrive at the farm in extreme misery. They had soon squandered their three thousand piastres, had separated, had reconciled, had quarreled again, had been thrown into jail, had escaped, and Friar Giroflée had at length turned Turk. Paquette had gone on plying her trade wherever she went, but made nothing out of it.

"I foresaw," said Martin to Candide, "that your gifts would soon be squandered and would only make them the more miserable. You have rolled in millions, you and Cacambo, and yet you are no happier than Friar Giroflée and Paquette."

"Ha!" said Pangloss to Paquette, "Providence has then brought you back among us, my poor child! Do you know that you cost me the tip of my nose, an eye, and an ear, as you can see? What a world this is!"
And this new adventure set them philosophizing more than ever.
In the neighborhood there lived a very famous Dervish, who was esteemed the best philosopher in all of Turkey, and they went to consult him. Pangloss was the spokesman.
"Master," he said, "we come to beg you to tell us why so strange an animal as man was made."
"What business is that of yours?" said the Dervish. "Is it your concern?"
"But, reverend father," said Candide, "there is horrible evil in this world."
"What does it matter," said the Dervish, "whether there is evil or good? When his highness sends a ship to Egypt, does he trouble himself over whether the mice on board are comfortable or not?"
"Then what must we do?" said Pangloss.
"Hold your tongue," answered the Dervish.

"I was hoping," said Pangloss, "that I might reason with you a little about causes and effects, about the best of all possible worlds, the origin of evil, the nature of the soul, and the pre-established harmony."
At these words, the Dervish shut the door in their faces.

During this conversation, news had spread that two Viziers and the Mufti had been strangled at Constantinople, and that several of their friends had been impaled. This catastrophe made a great noise for some hours. As Pangloss, Candide, and Martin returned to the little farm, they saw a good old man taking the fresh air at his door under a bower of orange trees. Pangloss, who was as inquisitive as he was argumentative, asked the old man what was the name of the strangled Mufti.

"I don't know," answered the worthy man, "and I have never known the name of any Mufti, or of any Vizier. I know nothing of the event you mention. I assume in general that those who meddle in the administration of public affairs sometimes die miserably, and that they deserve it; but I never concern myself about what is happening in Constantinople. I content myself with sending there for sale the fruits of the garden that I cultivate."

Having said these words, he invited the strangers into his house. His two sons and two daughters served them several kinds of sherbet, which they had made themselves, with kaimak enriched with candied citron peel, oranges, lemons, pineapples, pistachios, and Mocha coffee not adulterated with the bad coffee of Batavia or the American islands. After which the two daughters of the honest Muslim perfumed the strangers' beards.
"You must have a vast and magnificent estate," said Candide to the Turk.
"I have only twenty acres," replied the old man. "I and my children cultivate them. Our labor preserves us from three great evils—boredom, vice, and want."
On the way home, Candide reflected deeply on the old man's conversation.
"This honest Turk," he said to Pangloss and Martin, "seems to be in a situation far preferable to that of the six kings we had the honor of dining with."

"Grandeur," said Pangloss, "is extremely dangerous, according to the testimony of the philosophers. For, in short, Eglon, King of Moab, was assassinated by Ehud; Absalom was hanged by his hair and pierced with three darts; King Nadab, son of Jeroboam, was killed by Baasha; King Elah, by Zimri; Ahaziah, by Jehu; Athaliah, by Jehoiada; the Kings Jehoiakim, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah were carried off into captivity. You know how Croesus, Astyages, Darius, Dionysius of Syracuse, Pyrrhus, Perseus, Hannibal, Jugurtha, Ariovistus, Caesar, Pompey, Nero, Otho, Vitellius, Domitian, Richard II of England, Edward II, Henry VI, Richard III, Mary Stuart, Charles I, the three Henrys of France, and the Emperor Henry IV all perished. You know—"
"I know also," said Candide, "that we must cultivate our garden."
"You are right," said Pangloss, "for when man was first placed in the Garden of Eden, he was put there ut operaretur eum, that he might cultivate it; which shows that man was not born to be idle."
"Let us work," said Martin, "without arguing; it is the only way to make life tolerable."

The whole little society entered into this laudable plan, each according to his different abilities. Their little plot of land produced plentiful crops. Cunegonde was indeed very ugly, but she became an excellent pastry cook; Paquette worked at embroidery; the old woman took care of the linen. They were all, not excepting Friar Giroflée, of some use or other, for he made a good carpenter and became a very honest man.
Pangloss sometimes said to Candide:

"There is a concatenation of events in this best of all possible worlds: for if you had not been kicked out of a magnificent castle for the love of Miss Cunegonde, if you had not been put into the Inquisition, if you had not walked across America, if you had not run the Baron through the body, if you had not lost all your sheep from the fine country of El Dorado—you would not be here eating candied citron and pistachios."
"All that is very well," answered Candide, "but let us cultivate our garden."
